CHAPTER VI: SECTORAL TOURISM 
A. Ayurveda and Yoga Tourism 
6.1 The Committee notes the absence of Ayurveda in the Ministry’s tourism schemes and 
presentations, despite its significant potential, particularly in States such as Kerala and Tamil 
Nadu. Members observed that yoga tourism similarly lacks adequate focus despite global 
recognition. 
6.2 During the evidence, Members recommended that the Ministry work with Export Promotion 
Councils and the estimated 500-600 Ayurveda companies and practitioners to develop this 
segment. 
6.3 The Committee recommends that the Ministry formulate a dedicated promotion 
strategy for Ayurveda and yoga tourism in coordination with the Ministry of AYUSH and 
relevant Export Promotion Councils, with measurable targets for international wellness 
tourist arrivals. The strategy should include identification of 10-15 certified Ayurveda and 
yoga tourism destinations, standardisation of service quality, multilingual promotional 
content, and targeted outreach in key source markets with demonstrated demand for 
wellness tourism. 
B. Buddhist Circuit Development 
6.4 The Committee notes that the 2026-27 budget proposals include the development of 
Buddhist Circuits in Arunachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Assam, Manipur, Mizoram, and Tripura. 
Proposed interventions cover preservation of temples and monasteries, establishment of 
interpretation centres, improvement of pilgrim amenities, and strengthening of connectivity. 
6.5 The Committee observes that India attracts less than 1 per cent of the world’s Buddhist 
pilgrims despite being the birthplace of Buddhism and home to its most sacred sites. 
6.6 The Committee recommends that the Ministry prepare a time-bound action plan 
within three months for the Buddhist Tourist Circuit with measurable targets for 
international Buddhist pilgrim arrivals, developed in coordination with the Ministry of 
External Affairs and Indian missions in key Buddhist-majority countries including Japan, 
South Korea, Thailand, Myanmar, Sri Lanka, Vietnam, and Cambodia. The action plan 
should include targeted promotional campaigns, improvement of air and surface 
connectivity to Buddhist sites, dedicated interpretation services at all major Buddhist sites 
with multilingual capability, and institutional partnerships with Buddhist organisations 
and cultural bodies in source countries. 
C. Wildlife Tourism 
6.7 Members noted during the evidence that jungle tourism in India is among the most 
expensive globally, with expenditure of ₹8-10 lakh per visit at destinations such as 
Ranthambore. Members suggested focusing on specific national parks and tiger reserves rather 
than dispersing resources, citing Kaziranga as a potential model. 
 

13 
 
6.8 The Committee recommends that the Ministry develop a targeted strategy for wildlife 
tourism, identifying 10-15 high-potential national parks and tiger reserves for globally 
competitive positioning, in coordination with the Ministry of Environment, Forest and 
Climate Change. The strategy must include carrying capacity assessments, community 
benefit-sharing mechanisms, infrastructure improvement plans, and pricing 
rationalisation measures to enhance accessibility for both domestic and international 
tourists. 
D. Coastal and Blue Economy Tourism 
6.9 The Committee notes that several projects under SD 2.0, CBDD, PRASHAD, SASCI, and 
ACA relate to coastal and water-based tourism. The project “Alappuzha: A Global Water 
Wonderland” in Kerala (₹93.17 crore) is reported at 11.46 per cent physical completion. 
6.10 Cruise terminal projects at Mormugao (₹50.00 crore) and Mumbai (₹37.50 crore), and the 
Ex-INS Guldar Underwater Museum and Submarine Tourism project (₹46.91 crore), are noted 
by the Committee. 
6.11 The Committee recommends that the Ministry ensure close monitoring of all coastal 
and blue economy tourism projects for timely implementation. For cruise tourism, the 
Ministry should coordinate with the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways to develop 
a comprehensive cruise tourism facilitation framework, including streamlined immigration 
procedures, shore excursion infrastructure, and homeport development at selected ports. 
E. Eco-Tourism and Sustainable Tourism 
6.12 The Committee notes the Ministry’s formulation of National Strategies for Eco-tourism and 
Rural Tourism, and the Travel for LiFEprogramme. The 2026-27 proposals include development 
of Mountain Trails (Himachal Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Jammu and Kashmir, Araku Valley, and 
Podhigai Malai), Turtle Trails (Odisha, Karnataka, Kerala), and Bird Watching Trails (Pulikat 
Lake in Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu). 
6.13 When asked about Regenerative Tourism, the Ministry stated that this is a “comparatively 
newer concept” and no activities have been specifically proposed for 2026-27. 
6.14 The Committee recommends that the Ministry commission a study on regenerative 
tourism frameworks suitable for Indian conditions and integrate the findings into the 
design of schemes under the 16th Finance Commission cycle. The study should draw upon 
international best practices and be completed within one year. 
F. Medical Value Tourism 
6.15 The Ministry informed the Committee that the medical tourism sector does not fall directly 
under its mandate. The Ministry’s role is limited to branding and promotion. The 2026-27 
proposals include the establishment of five Regional Medical Hubs in partnership with the 
private sector, combining healthcare delivery, education, research facilities, AYUSH Centres, 
and Medical Value Tourism Facilitation Centres. 
 

14 
 
6.16 The Committee recommends that an inter-ministerial coordination mechanism for 
medical value tourism be formalised, involving the Ministry of Tourism, Ministry of 
Health and Family Welfare, Ministry of AYUSH, Ministry of Commerce and Industry, 
and the Ministry of Home Affairs. The mechanism should address standardisation of 
pricing transparency for foreign medical tourists, streamlined visa procedures, quality 
accreditation of participating hospitals, and a unified digital onboarding platform. 
G. Hotel Capacity and Pricing 
6.17 The Committee notes the hotel capacity constraints highlighted during the evidence. India 
has approximately 1,80,000 branded hotel rooms and 15,000 unbranded rooms. Industry 
estimates suggest approximately double this capacity is required. Members noted that room 
tariffs reach ₹12-13 lakh during major events and contrasted this with consistently affordable 
pricing in competing destinations such as Bangkok, where rooms remain available at ₹25,000-
45,000. 
6.18 The Ministry informed the Committee of efforts to reduce hotel licensing requirements 
from 50-90 permissions and to recommend the elimination of outdated regulations such as the 
Sarais Act. Tourism has been included for the first time in both central and state-level Ease of 
Doing Business frameworks. The NIDHI+ platform has recorded 55,414 registered 
accommodation units as of 23 January 2026. 
6.19 The Committee recommends that the Ministry coordinate with State Governments to 
address hotel capacity constraints through the following measures: (a) revision of Floor 
Area Ratio (FAR) norms for hotel development in all States with tourism potential; (b) 
expedited rationalisation of licensing requirements, with a target of reducing the number 
of permissions required to below 20 within two years; (c) repeal or replacement of the 
Sarais Act and other outdated regulations; and (d) inclusion of a hotel capacity 
augmentation component in the National Mission for 50 Globally Competitive 
Destinations. The Ministry may consider placing the progress report on each of these 
measures in the public domain. 
  

15 
 
CHAPTER VII: MANPOWER AND SKILL DEVELOPMENT 
A. Capacity Building for Service Providers 
7.1 Under the CBSP scheme, the Ministry trained 89,801 persons in 2024-25 through 
programmes covering language competency, etiquette, and communication skills. The HSRT 
(Hunar Se Rozgar Tak) courses are NSQF-approved skill development programmes. 
7.2 The Committee notes that 84 per cent of the tourism workforce operates in the informal 
sector without skill certification or training. The tourism and hospitality sector has a projected 
CAGR of 12-13 per cent. 
7.3 A total of ₹60 crore was allocated for skill development in 2025-26: ₹35 crore under 
Assistance to IHMs and ₹25 crore under CBSP. Under the IHM scheme, ₹20.10 crore had been 
utilised as of January 2026 (65 per cent of the RE of ₹31 crore). Under CBSP, the allocation was 
enhanced from ₹25 crore at BE to ₹80 crore at RE. 
7.4 The Committee recalls that in its earlier Report on “Holistic Development of India’s 
Tourism Sector through Formal Skill Development, University-Level Courses and Professional 
Training”, the Committee had observed that India’s challenge is not a shortage of destinations, 
but a shortage of credible interpreters of its civilisation, and had made detailed recommendations 
for addressing this gap. The Committee notes that several of these recommendations are directly 
relevant to the Demands for Grants under examination. 
7.5 The Committee recommends that the Ministry, in implementing the CBSP scheme and 
related training programmes for 2026-27, align its activities with the recommendations 
made in the Committee’s earlier Report, particularly with respect to: (a) the creation of a 
National Tourism Knowledge Grid with the IITTM as the academic anchor; (b) the 
deployment of a mission-mode Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) initiative to assess, 
train, and certify the informal workforce of guides, priests, and facilitators at the district 
level, as specifically recommended by the Committee; and (c) the incorporation of 
mandatory modules on Indian history, art, culture, geography, and interpretive 
storytelling in all tourism curricula. The Ministry may furnish a detailed action plan for 
implementation of these recommendations within three months. 
B. Paryatan Mitra / Paryatan Didi Initiative 
7.6 The Paryatan Mitra / Paryatan Didi initiative trained 4,382 individuals across 7 pilot 
destinations: Orchha, Gandikota, Bodh Gaya, Aizawl, Jodhpur, Srinagar, and Sri Vijaya Puram. 
The Ministry clarified that this training targets persons already engaged in tourism-related 
occupations and is designed for skill and behaviour modification. The Ministry stated that the 
question of placement rates is therefore not applicable. 
7.7 The Committee recommends that the Ministry expand the Paryatan Mitra / Paryatan 
Didi initiative beyond the current 7 pilot destinations to cover at least 50 destinations in 
2026-27, with a particular focus on the 50 destinations proposed under the National 
Mission. The Ministry should establish a tracking mechanism for measuring the impact of 
training on visitor satisfaction and service quality at trained destinations. 

16 
 
C. Tourist Guide Training 
7.8 The Ministry has announced plans to train 10,000 tourist guides across 20 iconic destinations 
through collaboration with IIMs, using a 12-week hybrid training course. 
7.9 During the evidence, Members questioned the need for IIM-level curriculum for tourist 
guides, when practical language training and cultural knowledge should suffice. Members cited 
examples from Spain, Thailand, and Cambodia, where retired teachers and ordinary citizens 
serve as guides effectively. 
7.10 The Committee recalls its earlier Report, in which it had recommended the notification of a 
new professional category titled “Certified Civilisational Interpreter (CCI)”, distinct from 
general tour guides, trained to provide historically rigorous, evidence-based interpretation 
supported by a tiered certification system linked to academic depth and language proficiency. 
7.11 The Committee recommends that the Ministry present the detailed training plan for 
the proposed 10,000 tourist guides, including budget allocation, pedagogical rationale, and 
justification for the IIM collaboration, before the programme is expanded. The Committee 
further recommends that the Ministry simultaneously advance the notification of the 
“Certified Civilisational Interpreter” cadre as recommended in the Committee’s earlier 
Report, ensuring that this professional category is distinct from general tour guides and is 
supported by a tiered certification system, multilingual capability assessment, and periodic 
renewal requirements. The Committee also reiterates its earlier recommendation that 
targeted incentives, including stipends or higher certification tiers, be provided for 
proficiency in UN and key emerging market languages such as Spanish, French, 
Mandarin, and Arabic. The Committee would further suggest that, in selecting an 
academic collaborator for the tourist guide training programme, the Ministry may 
consider whether a liberal arts curriculum, of the kind offered by institutions such as IIM 
Kozhikode or other reputable institutes with dedicated liberal arts and humanities 
programmes, may be more appropriate than a conventional management curriculum, 
given that the interpretive and communicative skills required of a tourist guide are more 
closely aligned with history, cultural studies, and the humanities than with business 
administration. The Committee would invite the Ministry to clarify whether management 
graduates trained in tourism-specific courses would in practice take up tourist guide 
professions, and to design the training architecture accordingly. 
D. Status of Institutes of Hotel Management 
7.12 Members raised concerns about State IHMs being closed (including in Yamuna Nagar, 
Haryana) without proper tracking of central government investments. 
7.13 The Committee notes that the Ministry has signed 70 Memoranda of Understanding 
between 10 leading hospitality chains and 21 Central IHMs. The Ministry has also proposed 
upgrading the National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology (NCHMCT) 
into a National Institute of Hospitality. 
 
7.14 Members specifically noted the absence of hotel management, hospitality, and tourist guide 
training institutions in the North-Eastern region beyond Guwahati. 

17 
 
7.15 The Committee recommends that the Ministry: (a) conduct audits of all State IHM 
closures and furnish an accountability report to the Committee within three months, 
indicating the amount of central investment in each closed institution and its current 
status; (b) prioritise the establishment of training institutions throughout the North-
Eastern region, aligned with the ₹233.60 crore allocation for NE tourism infrastructure 
and the proposed Buddhist Circuits; and (c) ensure that the proposed National Institute of 
Hospitality, once established, serves as a vehicle for international institutional 
partnerships, including faculty exchange, curriculum benchmarking, and mutual 
recognition of qualifications with leading hospitality institutes abroad, as recommended by 
the Committee in Chapter V of this Report. 
E. Industry Immersion and Prior Learning Recognition 
7.16 The Committee recalls that in its earlier Report, the Committee had recommended that all 
tourism degree and diploma programmes include a mandatory paid industry immersion module 
of three to six months, jointly assessed by academic faculty and industry mentors, with 
institutional grants linked to graduate employment outcomes. The Committee had further 
recommended a mission-mode Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) initiative to assess, train, 
and certify the existing informal workforce of guides, priests, and facilitators at the district level, 
with verifiable digital certifications renewed periodically. 
7.17 The Committee reiterates these recommendations and urges the Ministry to report on 
the action taken for their implementation within three months of the presentation of this 
Report. The Committee further recommends that the ASI be formally partnered with the 
proposed training framework for the training of site guides, with the ASI continuing as the 
custodian of factual accuracy while educational institutions handle content delivery and 
pedagogical aspects, as specifically recommended in the Committee’s earlier Report. 
F. Divyangjan Kaushal Yojana 
7.18 The Committee notes the proposed skill development interventions for Divyangjan in the 
hospitality and food and beverages sectors. 
7.19 The Committee recommends that training modules be customised for specific 
categories of disability, with a clear pathway to employment and industry integration. The 
Ministry may report progress on this initiative to the Committee within three months. 
G. Dedicated Budget for Manpower Development 
7.20 The Committee recalls its earlier recommendation for the creation of a dedicated budgetary 
sub-head for Human Capital Development within the Ministry of Tourism’s budget, to ensure 
that funds earmarked for training are not diverted to infrastructure or publicity activities. The 
Committee had further proposed a voluntary or matched-funding contribution model from 
industry partners. 
7.21 The Committee reiterates this recommendation and urges the Ministry to take steps 
for the creation of such a dedicated sub-head from the financial year 2027-28 onwards. 
The Ministry may also explore and report on the feasibility of a matched-funding model 
with industry partners within three months. 

18 
 
CHAPTER VIII: DIGITAL INITIATIVES 
8.1 The Committee notes the revamped Incredible India Digital Platform (IIDP), which serves as 
a digital repository of tourism content covering heritage sites, cultural circuits, festivals, and 
travel services. During 2025-26, the IIDP recorded approximately 37 lakh visitors. 
8.2 The platform incorporates an AI-enabled tool for personalisation, provides real-time weather 
updates and city guides, and has partnered with Online Travel Agents (OTAs) for booking 
services including flights, hotels, cabs, buses, and entry tickets for ASI monuments. The 
Incredible India Content Hub provides promotional materials for stakeholders. 
8.3 The Ministry has proposed establishing a National Destination Digital Knowledge Grid for 
digital documentation of sites of cultural, spiritual, and heritage significance. 
8.4 The Committee recalls that in its earlier Report, the Committee had recommended that the 
Government prioritise technology-aided interpretation, including audio guides and augmented or 
virtual reality tools, developed to the same content standards as human training. 
8.5 The Committee recommends that the Ministry: (a) set measurable annual targets for 
IIDP user engagement and benchmark performance against comparable national tourism 
platforms globally, with the aim of increasing the user base from the current 37 lakh to at 
least 1 crore visitors within two years; (b) operationalise the National Destination Digital 
Knowledge Grid with the participation of local researchers, historians, content creators, 
and technology partners, as recommended in the Committee’s earlier Report; (c) develop 
and deploy technology-aided interpretation tools, including audio guides in at least 10 
languages and augmented/virtual reality experiences at 20 major heritage sites, within the 
2026-27 fiscal year; and (d) integrate the IIDP with social media and influencer outreach 
strategies for wider reach. The Ministry may report progress on each of these targets to 
the Committee within three months. 
  

19 
 
CHAPTER IX: INSTITUTIONAL AND GOVERNANCE ISSUES 
A. Constitutional Status of Tourism 
9.1 The Committee notes that tourism is neither in the Union List, the State List, nor the 
Concurrent List of the Constitution and is treated as a residual subject. Members observed 
during the evidence that this creates inherent coordination difficulties between the Centre and 
the States. The question raised by Members during the evidence, regarding whether tourism is 
the responsibility of the Centre or the States, reflects a persistent structural ambiguity. 
9.2 The Committee recommends that the Ministry, in consultation with NITI Aayog, 
prepare a comprehensive policy note examining mechanisms to strengthen Centre-State 
coordination for tourism, including the feasibility of including tourism in the Concurrent 
List or establishing a statutory National Tourism Authority with defined roles, 
responsibilities, and enforcement powers. The policy note may be submitted to the 
Committee within one year. 
B. Staffing and Institutional Capacity 
9.3 The Committee notes that the Ministry operates with a vacancy rate of approximately 35 per 
cent, with 359 personnel in position against a sanctioned strength of 552. 
9.4 The Committee recommends the preparation of a time-bound recruitment plan to fill 
all vacant posts within one financial year. The Ministry may furnish the recruitment plan 
to the Committee within three months. 
C. Outstanding Audit Paragraphs 
9.5 As of 17 February 2026, 21 C&AG audit paragraphs remain pending against the Ministry, 
spanning the years 2021 to 2025. Subjects covered include significant savings at the minor/sub-
head level, the functioning of the Indian Culinary Institute, the Swadesh Darshan scheme, loss to 
the Government exchequer, non-surrender of savings, blocking of funds for setting up of State 
Institute of Hotel Management (Kottayam), blocking of funds due to non-setting up of Food 
Craft Institute, expenditure without a budget line, and outstanding utilisation certificates. 
9.6 The Committee recommends that the Ministry constitute a dedicated Audit Settlement 
Cell for the purpose of settling all 21 pending C&AG audit paragraphs within six months. 
The Ministry may furnish a status report on progress in settlement of these paragraphs to 
the Committee on a quarterly basis. 
D. Multi-Departmental Coordination 
9.7 Members observed during the evidence that tourism requires coordination across multiple 
Ministries, including transport, highways, immigration, civil aviation, health, AYUSH, and 
external affairs. The tourism Ministry, however, lacks authority over these domains. 
9.8 The Committee notes the Ministry’s efforts to coordinate with the Ministry of Civil Aviation 
regarding the Modified UDAN scheme, ATF VAT reduction (letters sent to the State 
Governments of Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Kerala, West Bengal, and Jharkhand), and 

20 
 
integration of tourism-priority destinations with HML infrastructure and PLI frameworks. The 
Ministry has also proposed a list of tourism-potential air routes to the Ministry of Civil Aviation. 
9.9 The Committee recommends that inter-ministerial coordination be institutionalised 
through a permanent Tourism Coordination Committee at the Secretary level, meeting at 
least quarterly, with representation from the Ministries of Tourism, Civil Aviation, 
External Affairs, Home Affairs, Health and Family Welfare, AYUSH, Culture, and 
Railways. The Committee may be informed of the constitution and proceedings of this 
body. 
E. Non-Implementation of Previous Committee Recommendations 
9.10 The Committee records that Members expressed concern during the evidence that 
Committee recommendations have not been acted upon and no Action Taken Reports have been 
provided despite proceedings over the past 12 years. One Member called for a formal 
mechanism to track the Ministry’s compliance with Committee recommendations. 
9.11 The Committee directs the Ministry to submit comprehensive Action Taken Reports 
on all recommendations made in the preceding three Committee reports within 90 days of 
the presentation of this Report. The Committee views the non-submission of Action Taken 
Reports over such an extended period as a serious matter and expects full compliance. 
F. Ministry Presentations 
9.12 Several senior Members noted during the evidence that the Ministry’s presentation 
photographs and content have remained unchanged for 10-12 years. 
9.13 The Committee expects that all future presentations to the Committee reflect updated 
data, new project outcomes, current strategic priorities, and evidence of implementation of 
the Committee’s recommendations. The Ministry shall not present recycled content or 
previously used presentation material. 
G. Industry Status for Tourism 
9.14 The Committee notes that 25 States/UTs have granted industry status to the tourism sector, 
namely: Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Goa, Gujarat, Haryana, Himachal 
Pradesh, Jammu and Kashmir, Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, 
Nagaland, Odisha, Puducherry, Punjab, Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Tripura, Uttar Pradesh, 
Uttarakhand, and West Bengal. The Ministry launched a Handbook on Industry Status in 
September 2024. 
9.15 The Committee recommends that the Ministry engage with the remaining States and 
UTs that have not yet granted industry status, including Madhya Pradesh, Telangana, 
Sikkim, Delhi, Ladakh, Lakshadweep, Andaman and Nicobar Islands, Dadra and Nagar 
Haveli and Daman and Diu, and Chandigarh, and report progress to the Committee within 
three months. 
  

21 
 
CHAPTER X: FUTURE PLANS 
A. Scheme Rationalisation for the 16th Finance Commission Cycle 
10.1 The Ministry has proposed consolidating eight current schemes into three integrated 
schemes for the 16th Finance Commission cycle (2026-31): 
(a) National Mission for 50 Globally Competitive Destinations: proposed outlay of ₹25,000 
crore over five years, to be implemented through Destination Management Organisations 
(DMOs) with performance-based incentives and private sector participation. 
(b) Unified Tourism Infrastructure Development Scheme: consolidating Swadesh Darshan, 
PRASHAD, and other assistance programmes. 
(c) Integrated Promotion and Publicity Scheme: merging overseas and domestic promotion with 
a proposed outlay of ₹5,000 crore over five years. 
10.2 The Committee notes that the proposed National Mission implies an annual expenditure 
capacity of approximately ₹5,000 crore, which is roughly double the Ministry’s current demand. 
10.3 The Committee recommends that all EFC notes for new schemes under the 16th 
Finance Commission cycle be accompanied by: (a) detailed implementation roadmaps with 
year-wise milestones; (b) institutional capacity assessments; (c) State-wise absorption plans 
based on past expenditure performance; (d) a phased scaling mechanism linked to 
demonstrated expenditure performance; and (e) a clear human resource plan, addressing 
the current 35 per cent vacancy rate, to ensure adequate supervisory capacity for the 
expanded outlay. The Committee further recommends that the Unified Tourism 
Infrastructure Development Scheme incorporate specific provisions for post-project 
maintenance, asset management, and regular third-party impact assessments. 
B. Key Initiatives Proposed for 2026-27 
10.4 The Ministry has informed the Committee of the following initiatives proposed for 2026-
27: (a) Development of 15 identified archaeological sites, including Lothal, Dholavira, 
Rakhigarhi, Adichanallur, Sarnath, Hastinapur, and Leh Palace. (b) Seaplane connectivity and 
Viability Gap Funding (VGF) for remote and water-linked destinations, with incentives for 
indigenous manufacturing of seaplanes. (c) Reduction of TCS on overseas tour programme 
packages to 2 per cent. (d) Development of Buddhist Circuits in the North-Eastern region. (e) 
Establishment of five Regional Medical Hubs. (f) National Destination Digital Knowledge Grid. 
(g) Divyangjan Kaushal Yojana for the hospitality sector. (h) Development of Eco-Tourism and 
Nature-Based Trails. (i) Development of tourism destinations in Purvodaya States. 
10.5 The Committee notes these proposals and recommends that the Ministry furnish a 
progress report on each initiative, including physical and financial milestones achieved, 
within three months of the presentation of this Report. 
C. National Awards for Tourism Professionals 
10.6 The Committee recalls its earlier recommendation for the institution of National Awards 
for “Best Civilisational Interpreter” and “Best Heritage Storyteller”, to be presented annually 
alongside existing National Tourism Awards. 

22 
 
10.7 The Committee reiterates this recommendation and urges the Ministry to institute 
these awards from the year 2026-27, with a view to elevating the professional status and 
public recognition of tourism interpreters. Such recognition, combined with clear career 
pathways, will strengthen India’s interpretive workforce and position Indian tourism 
professionals as credible representatives of the country’s heritage. 
D. Tourism Satellite Account 
10.8 The Committee notes that a Tourism Satellite Account (TSA) is the internationally 
recognised framework, recommended by the United Nations World Tourism Organisation, for 
measuring the economic contribution of tourism in a manner comparable across countries. India 
has compiled three TSAs to date: the first for 2002-03, the second for 2009-10, and the third for 
2015-16, all prepared by the National Council of Applied Economic Research (NCAER) for the 
Ministry of Tourism. The most recent TSA is now nearly a decade old. The absence of a current 
TSA weakens the evidentiary basis for the Ministry’s resource claims, limits India’s ability to 
benchmark its tourism economy against international comparators, and prevents accurate 
attribution of tourism-related employment, income, and value addition across sub-sectors. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry take steps, in coordination with the Ministry of 
Statistics and Programme Implementation, to ensure that a fully updated TSA is compiled 
and published at regular intervals not exceeding five years, and that the findings are 
incorporated into the Ministry’s budgetary presentations and policy planning. The 
Ministry may place a note on the status and roadmap for the Tourism Satellite Account 
before the Committee within three months.

CHAPTER XI: SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS 
The following is a consolidated summary of the recommendations made by the Committee in 
the preceding chapters. For full context, the relevant chapter and paragraph references are 
indicated. 
Recommendation 1 (Para 1.4): The Committee recommends that the Ministry take immediate 
steps to secure the required allocation for promotional activities through appropriate budgetary 
means, including a Supplementary Demand, and ensure that a structured multi-year promotional 
budget is established from the next financial year onwards. 
Recommendation 2 (Para 1.4A): The Committee recommends the setting-up of an India 
Tourism Promotion Board, ring-fencing of the OPP budget as a committed multi-year line, and 
appointment of designated Tourism Officers within Indian Embassies and High Commissions in 
key source markets. 
Recommendation 3 (Para 1.11): The Committee recommends that the Ministry implement a 
mandatory quarterly expenditure schedule targeting a minimum of 20 per cent utilisation in Q1, 
25 per cent in Q2, and 30 per cent in Q3. A digitalisedUtilisation Certificate submission portal 
must be established within three months. The Ministry may submit quarterly utilisation reports 
to the Committee. 
Recommendation 4 (Para 1.13): The Committee recommends that any future projections to the 
Ministry of Finance be accompanied by a detailed expenditure performance statement for the 
preceding three years, along with specific measures proposed to improve utilisation. 
Recommendation 5 (Para 2.7): The Committee recommends that the Ministry publish a 
quarterly, project-wise implementation status report for all Swadesh Darshan and CBDD 
projects, institute a formal mechanism for linking future project sanctions to past State 
performance, and furnish within three months a detailed assessment of the 77 projects currently 
below 25 per cent progress. 
Recommendation 6 (Para 2.11): The Committee recommends that for all new PRASHAD 
project sanctions, clear land titles and inter-agency clearances be enforced as non-negotiable 
prerequisites. A standard operating procedure for deviation requests, with a timeline of 30 days, 
must be formulated. 
Recommendation 7 (Para 2.15): The Committee recommends that the Ministry treat the 
pending DoE concurrence for PM-JUGA projects as a matter of utmost urgency, review and

Recommendation 8 (Para 2.18): The Committee recommends formalisation of inter-agency

We were opposed to the introduction of ·the Air Corporations (Transfer of Undertakings 
and Repeal) Bill, which was introduced in the Lok Sabha on 4th May, 1992.

the International Monetary fund. seeks to subvert the self-reliant economy of the count ry , 
dasmember the Public Secto r and em bark upon the path of unbriadled privatisation. 
The Air Corporations Act of 1953. which is being sought to be repealed by the present 
Ball, was enacted in keeping with the Industrial Policy Statement of 1948 and got funher 
impetus by the fndustrial Policy Resolution of 1956, which called for giving a commandeer · 
ing role to the Public Sector by identifying several core sectors of industries to be rC$erved 
for Public Sector for the growth and development of a self-reliant national economy. The 
Air Corporations A~t of !953 served as a correct precursor to this policy by reserving the air 
traffic for the Publi c Sector . This is so vital not only for the growth of national economy but 
aho for the security and defence of the country. 
Over the years the t wo Corpora tions, viz. the Indian Airlines and Air India did register 
impressive growth und contributed to the national economy and safety of the country . For 
the growth of a self-reliant economy and safety and defence of the coun try, it is necessary 
that Bud getary support h;as to be provided to the two Corporations. 
We are tlterefore totally opposed to the Bill, in its entirety, which seeks to repeal the Air 
Corporations Act and thereby clear the path for privatisation of the air traffic, including by 
foreign air liners, enua ngering the defence of the country, its soverei gnty and exposing it to 
imperi;alist machinations.

INTRODUCTION
            I, the Chairman, Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport & Tourism, having been authorised by the
 Committee to present on their behalf, present this Fortieth Report on “Problems faced by Tourists/Passengers at the
 Airports in the Country”.
2.         The Committee at its meeting held on 18
th January 1999, 22nd January 1999 & 27th January 1999 considered the
 subject and took evidence of representatives of Ministry of Civil Aviation, Ministry of Home Affairs, Ministry of
 Finance, Airports Authority of India and Tour & Travel Agencies.
3.         The Committee wish to express its thanks to the officers of Ministry of Civil Aviation, Ministry of Home
 Affairs, Ministry of Finance, Airports Authority of India and representatives of Tour & Travel Agencies for placing
 before the Committee the material and information desired in connection with the subject and for giving evidence
 before the Committee.
4.         The Committee at its meeting held on the 1
st March 2000 considered and adopted the Report.
NEW DELHI                                                                                                                 MD. SALIM
March, 1, 2000                                                                                                                 Chairman
Phalguna 11, 1921 (Saka)                                                                           Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Transport & Tourism
 
 
REPORT
 
The Committee on Transport and Tourism, at its meeting held on Tuesday, the 11th August 1998, decided to undertake
 the examination of the problems faced by both the foreign & domestic passengers/tourists at the airports while
 negotiating various mandatory clearances like Customs/Immigration/Visa/Foreign exchange etc.  Besides this, the
 Committee felt that the travelling public also encounters problems in the use of several facilities like
 Transport/Luggage Trolleys, toilets, drinking water, restaurants, medical aid, enquiry counter for assistance etc.  The
 Committee is of the view that the general opinion about the functioning of the airports amongst the travelling public is
 very poor.  The services provided at the airport are not upto the mark as compared to international standards and as
 such these need adequate improvements.
2.            Keeping in view the public importance of the subject, the Committee on Transport and Tourism issued
 advertisements in the leading newspapers all over the country as well as on Doordarshan/All India Radio seeking
 personal experience, suggestions of the public and views of the leading tour and travel operators regarding the
 difficulties/ harassment faced by the foreign/domestic passengers/tourists in availing the various facilities like visa,
 customs, immigration, foreign exchange, transport, shopping, security, general amenities etc. presently made available
 at the airports in the country.
3.         The advertisement issued in the newspapers/Doordarshan/All India Radio evoked encouraging response from the
 general public as well as from the leading Tour & Travel operators.  A total number of 132 memoranda were received
 containing the personal experiences of the travelling public and suggestions for improvements in the running of the
 airports.
4.         The Committee held discussions with the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Airports Authority of India.  The
 Committee also heard the views of the Ministries of Home Affairs, Finance (Department of Revenue) and External
 Affairs, which are directly related to the management of many mandatory clearances, which a tourist has to obtain at
 the international airports in the country.
5.         The Committee also heard the views of leading Tour & Travel operators/Agencies and individuals on the
 subject.
6.         The Committee on Transport and Tourism visited Airports at Delhi, Mumbai, Goa, Chennai,
 Thiruvananthapuram, Guwahati and Ahmedabad to examine the functioning of these Airports and the facilities
 provided to the tourists at the airports.
The Committee was informed by the Airports Authority of India that they provide only tourism related facilities to the
 tourists at the airports which consists of paid/free facilities.
The Committee was also informed by the AAI that it manages five International airports namely Mumbai, Delhi,
 Chennai, Calcutta and Thiruvananthapuram, 87 Domestic airports and 28 Civil Air Terminals at Defence Airfields, a
 total of 120 airports in the country.
The Committee, after careful examination of the memoranda received by it and hearing the views of the concerned

The Committee on Transport and Tourism, at its meeting held on Tuesday, the 11th August 1998, decided to undertake the examina
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/40threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:45:03]
 Ministries, Tour & Travel operators and individuals, came to the conclusion that the major areas which require
 improvement at the airports are lack of co-ordination amongst the various agencies functioning at the airports,
 overcrowding of the departure/arrival lounges, harassment of tourists in obtaining immigration, visa/customs clearance,
 wearing of uniform by the staff working at the airports for their proper identification, transport facility and problem of
 touts, lack of civic amenities and etiquette and behaviour of the staff at the airports, shortage of luggage trolleys etc.
 
CO-ORDINATION AMONGST VARIOUS AGENCIES AT AIRPORTS
The Committee was informed by the Airports Authority of India that a large number of organisations are working at the
 airports and AAI is one of them.  The main agencies working at the airports, particularly at the international airports,
 are customs, foreign exchange department controlled by the Ministry of Finance, visa under the Ministry of External
 Affairs and immigration and security with the Ministry of Home Affairs.  It was further explained to the Committee
 that the AAI does not exercise kind of control over these agencies and it only provides working space to them.  The
 Committee observed that there is a complete lack of            co-ordination amongst the various agencies/organisations
 working at the airports, particularly at the international airports, due to which the travelling public in general and
 tourists in particular, face a lot of problems as they do not know which single authority they should approach in case of
 any problem.   They have to go separately to each department for the redressal of their problems/complaints and every
 department/official shift its responsibility upon others.  The question of bestowing special powers to the Airport
 Director to enable him to have a better grip on the situation at the airport was also suggested as a possible solution to
 the lack of co-ordination.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be one working officer posted at
 the airports for maintaining efficient co-ordination amongst all the agencies viz. Customs, immigration, visa, security,
 foreign exchange etc. operating at the international airports.  This power should be vested with the Airport Director, as
 this would go a long way in streamlining the management of the airports.  To have greater transparency at the airports,
 there should be a Central Control Room supervised by the Airport Director where the passengers could lodge their
 grievances/complaints in respect of any of the agencies functioning at an airport.  The proposed Central Control Room
 should also be equipped to handle any emergency situation.  The Committee further recommends that to make the
 airports more user friendly, an advisory committee, on the lines of Railways Advisory Committee, may be constituted
 at all the airports comprising of officials of the agencies functioning at the airports and the representatives of general
 public.
 
IMMIGRATION/STAMPING OF PASSPORTS
The Committee was informed that it takes a lot of time at the immigration counters for passengers to obtain clearance. 
 The problem is further aggravated due to bunching of flights at night, which leads to more delay in getting clearance. 
 The representative of the Ministry of Home Affairs informed the Committee during evidence that in 95% cases,
 clearance is done in 30 minutes and in only 5% cases, the time taken is 45 minutes.  The international prescribed
 standard clearance time on arrival of the passengers is 45 minutes.  The Committee was also informed that a proposal
 relating to computerisation of passport office is also under consideration so that machine-readable passports could be
 issued in future.  For this comprehensive computerisation proposal, the Ministry has taken the advice of the Department
 of Electronics, as it is a technical subject. The Committee was also informed that at our airports, each regulatory agency
 viz. Customs, Immigration and Security compulsorily stamps the boarding card after check of each and every
 passenger, and this stamping is further checked subsequently by these regulatory agencies, thus making a passenger to
 stop at many places before proceeding for boarding.  At most international airports, none of the agencies stamp the
 boarding card, thus, passenger is not required to stop at different points and his flow becomes smooth. 
 The Committee is of the view that 30-45 minutes is a long time for the passengers of a flight to be cleared.  The
 Government should make efforts to reduce this time to 15-20 minutes.  Steps should be taken to open more counters,
 especially during nights when there is bunching of flights.  The Committee appreciates the proposal of computerisation
 of passports office and issue of machine readable passports and recommends that the matter should not be delayed
 much so that machine readable passport facility can be introduced at the earliest in order to reduce the checking time at
 immigration counter and till this takes place, the Ministry of Home Affairs, in consultation with the AAI, should ensure
 speedy clearance of the passengers by opening more counters.  As regards the stamping of passports, the Committee
 observes that a streamlining of these regulatory procedures would go a long way in reducing passenger fatigue, tension
 and resultant problems to passengers, especially tourists, who are used to much simpler departure procedures at other
 international airports.
The Committee was informed that in several countries the citizens of those countries holding a valid passport are not
 required to pass through the immigration counter whenever they return home country after visiting a foreign country. 

The Committee on Transport and Tourism, at its meeting held on Tuesday, the 11th August 1998, decided to undertake the examina
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/40threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:45:03]
 The representatives of the Ministry of Home Affairs also informed the Committee that simplification of immigration
 formalities is under the active consideration of the Government and the Ministry of Law has accorded clearance for
 these proposals.  The Committee desires that the matter should be got expedited so that necessary notification should be
 issued to make immigration clearance easier both for the foreign tourists as well as for the Indian passport holders
 returning their home country.
 
VIDEO MONITORING OF THE MAIN AREAS OF THE AIRPORT
During its discussion with the various tour & travel operators and individuals, the Committee was informed that a lot of
 overcrowding takes place at the airport especially at the halls where immigration/custom/visa counters are functioning. 
 The problem is further worsened when there is a bunching of flights.  The Committee was also informed that a tourist
 also suffers a lot of harassment and inconvenience due to this overcrowding as it leads to long delays and also by the
 malpractices indulged in by the official/staff working on these counters.  The Committee was surprised to know that at
 present no regular monitoring at the airport is being done with the help of video cameras/CCTV.  The officers incharge
 at these organisations posted at the airport are some times not even aware of the problems of overcrowding taking place
 at their respective counters.  Therefore, they are not able to take timely action to cope up with the situation. The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that all international airport should be equipped with video monitoring system
 which should be kept working for twenty four hours at all the public handling areas viz. Immigration, Visa and Custom
 counter in arrival/departure halls/lounges and that this monitoring should be done at one centralised place where a high
 ranking officer can monitor immigration/custom/visa/baggage areas.  The person handling the video monitoring should
 immediately inform the concerned agency/officer in case he notices any overcrowding and malpractice being indulged
 in by the staff manning a particular counter.  The authority/representative of the Ministry should be more vigilant in
 taking action promptly.
 
WORKING OF ESCALATORS AT THE AIRPORTS
The Committee was unhappy with the recent escalator incident at the Indira Gandhi International Airport in which a
 minor girl was crushed to death and that no official/doctor attended the girl for a long time.  During its visit to the
 airport, the Committee noted that the escalator had not become operational even after two months of the incident,
 resulting in inconvenience to passengers, especially old people, ladies and children.  The Committee was informed by
 the AAI that it was not made operational due to the enquiry in process into the escalator accident.  The Committee,
 however, recommends that the escalator at IGI airport may be put into operation immediately in order to avoid
 inconvenience to the passengers.  The Committee further recommends that the escalators installed at the airports should
 be properly maintained and the same should be regularly monitored.  It is also recommended that in view of the
 increase in passenger load, the escalators should be fitted with latest security equipments and safety measures.  The
 officials posted near the escalators should be aware of the switches that could be switched off in case of emergencies. 
 The Committee feels that the airport management should be ready to deal with any emergency situation and that
 response time to emergency situations must improve.
 
WEARING OF UNIFORM BY THE STAFF AT AIRPORTS
It has come to the notice of the Committee that officials working at the airports come on duty without their uniforms,
 which causes a lot of inconvenience to the passengers with respect to their identification.  The Committee was further
 informed by the Ministry of Home Affairs that the immigration officers are being paid uniform allowance @ Rs.750/-
 p.m.  However, since this rate is very less they have requested the Ministry of Finance for enhancement of this amount
 from Rs.750/- to Rs.2900/- per month but the Ministry of Finance has rejected their proposal.
The Committee feels that the uniform of the officials shows discipline of any organisation.  However, it is also of the
 view that the uniforms allowance, which is at present being paid, is very meagre and needs enhancement.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Home Affairs should take up this matter with the Ministry
 of Finance for reconsideration of their proposal relating to increase in uniform allowance.  It further recommends that
 uniform should be provided to each of them and it should be made compulsory to wear. 
It is also recommended that instead of identity badges, the names of the officials should be embroidered, in big letters,
 on the uniforms of the officials.  They should also be directed to display the identity card on their uniform, which not
 only gives an impressive look but also helps one to recognise them easily in case of need.
 
CUSTOMS
The Committee was satisfied by the services provided by the custom department.  However, it observed that some

 custom officers insist upon the passengers to open their suitcases even after X-ray of the baggage has been done.  The
 passengers find it difficult to repack their baggages.  The passengers also face a lot of problems while passing through
 the red channel.  The Committee also observed that generally Custom officials look at the passengers with suspicion
 specially the labour class coming from gulf countries.  As labour class is less educated they do not have much idea
 about the articles that are allowed to be brought or not.  They also do not know how much duty could be levied on the
 articles carried by them.  The lack of knowledge of rules in this regard results in their harassment by the customs
 officials and some times they have to pay money to get cleared their baggage.  The Committee was also of the view that
 neither Indian Airlines nor Air India or for that matter any other personnel working at the airports have any knowledge
 about the baggage rules or custom rules.
The Committee was further informed by the representatives of the Ministry of Finance that they publish a book called
 “Guide for Travellers” relating to customs regulations for travellers and they also circulate this book.  The Committee
 observed that many people do not know about this book and therefore, recommends that ‘Guide for Travellers’ should
 be made available to all the passengers/tourists at all the international airports not only in Hindi but also in English and
 in local languages so that less educated passengers from different parts of the country and abroad can understand the
 rules relating to customs regulations for passengers.  The Committee also suggests that physical checking of baggage
 should not be done on a discriminatory basis and it should be based on some rationale and be reduced to the minimum
 to avoid harassment to the passengers.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that a booklet containing relevant
 information like financial limit, what goods one can bring, what are the items for which the passenger should go
 through the red channel, on which articles custom duties can be imposed etc. should be given to the airlines at airports
 and may be kept at other places also.  It can also be attached with dis-embarkation card so that an average passenger
 can be aware of custom rules and regulations.
 
FRISKING
The Committee was informed that at the Indian airports, manual frisking is carried out for each and every passenger,
 instead of using sophisticated modern equipments.  Consequently, the passengers at the airports have to wait for a long
 time in a queue for their security check.  The Committee recommends that the security arrangements for frisking should
 be thoroughly modernised so that dependence on manual checking is reduced to the minimum.  Placing more reliance
 on modern security equipments would expedite security checks and reduce long waiting time and congestion outside
 the security hold areas.  Security personnel carrying out physical search should be friendly and courteous.
HAJ TERMINAL
During its visit to the Indira Gandhi International Airport at Delhi, the Committee visited the newly constructed Haj
 Terminal.  The Committee was informed that the Terminal would serve as a single point area for the departure and
 arrival of Haj Pilgrims.  The Committee noted that outside the terminal, there were no sheds/tents for taking rest by the
 relatives who had come to receive and see off the Haj pilgrims.  The Committee also noted that there was lack of basic
 facilities like drinking water, toilets, canteen etc. outside the Terminal.
The Committee appreciates the construction of a new Haj Terminal at Delhi by the Airports Authority of India for the
 benefit of Haj pilgrims.  The Committee feels that the new Haj Terminal would help in smooth and expeditious
 clearance of Haj pilgrims.  The Government may explore the possibility of having such Haj Terminals catering to Haj
 flights at other airports also.  However, the Committee recommends that some shed etc. may be constructed outside the
 Terminal at IGI airport at the earliest.  Immediate steps may also be taken to provide facilities for drinking water,
 toilets, canteen etc.
 
ETIQUETTES, BEHAVIOUR AND TRAINING OF THE STAFF
It has come to the notice of the Committee that the officials deputed at immigration & customs counter generally behave
 rudely with the passengers.  This type of behavior does not go well with the tourists and creates an unpleasant
 atmosphere.  Today national/international airports are gateways of any country.  The passenger/tourist gets first
 impression of a particular country at the airport itself, which represents the culture and society of any country, as the
 immigration counter is the first point of contact for any traveller.    A pleasant smile and courteous behavior of the
 airport officials can give a sense of relief to a person tired from the journeys.  The Committee, therefore, recommends
 that officials deputed at the airports, especially at the immigration/custom counters should be strictly asked to be
 courteous and behave good mannerly with the passengers.  The Committee is of the view that this could be done only
 by constant training and strict supervision.  A regular training, based on latest managerial and behaviour modules
 developed by consultants of national repute, should be imparted to the officials in dealing with the passengers/tourists
 to make them more tourists friendly.  The officials so trained would be better equipped to welcome the tourists with a

The Committee on Transport and Tourism, at its meeting held on Tuesday, the 11th August 1998, decided to undertake the examina
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/40threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:45:03]
 smile on their faces.  This would go a long way in creating a courteous atmosphere at the Airports.
 
TRANSPORT SYSTEM AT THE AIRPORT
During its interaction with the tours and travel operators, the Committee was apprised that when a passenger lands at the
 Airport he has to face a lot of problem in hiring Transport.  It was noticed by the Committee that pre-paid taxi counters
 had not been opened at some of the Airports.  If a counter is there, adequate number of taxis are not available to the
 passengers.  Taxis that are available at the airport are of 20-35 years old and are in bad condition.  Old people, ladies
 with children always face problem in getting taxis as they are not in a position to run with their baggage.  There is no
 display board mentioning the rates to be charged for various destinations, which always leaves the possibility of
 cheating, specially with the foreigners.  Taxi drivers are generally without uniform and identity badges. 
 Passengers/tourists are some times forcefully stopped and looted by the private taxi owners.  Sometimes passengers are
 not allowed to reach pre-paid taxi counters.  The Committee also noted that most of the Airports do not have their own
 carrier facilities for the passengers to reach their destination/airport.  The Committee was informed that AAI are
 running free buses for inter-terminals movements for passengers.  However, for their journeys outside the airports, it is
 done by other public transports or taxi services.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that pre-paid taxi counters at the airports should be increased and opened at all
 the airports in the country where this facility is not available.  The Government should make it compulsory that all the
 taxis, which operate at the airports, should be neat, clean and in good condition.  There should also be facility of air-
conditioned taxis for those passengers who prefer this mode of transport.  It should also be made compulsory for the taxi
 drivers to wear uniform and show their identity badges/names on the dress.  More counters of pre-paid taxis should be
 opened to avoid rush at one place and a queue system should be introduced and preference should be given to old
 people/ladies with children. Some police personnel should also be deputed at the prepaid taxi stands to ensure that the
 queue system functions properly.  A rate-list showing charges for various destinations within the city should be
 prominently displayed at the prepaid taxi counters.  A mechanism should be developed whereby the private taxis
 operating at the airports are not able to overcharge/cheat the passengers.  Private taxi owners should not be allowed
 inside the airport.  The Committee also suggests that AAI itself should make some arrangement for providing bus
 services at the minimum charges from the airport to the city.
The Committee has also been informed that parking area is not well connected with the arrival/departure halls at the
 airports.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that these areas should be well connected.
 
DUTY FREE SHOPS
The Committee noted that most of our airports are very congested and duty free shops at our international airports are
 limited in number with limited stock of items and there is also not enough space for the shopkeepers to demonstrate
 their wares. The Committee is of the view that since the shopping areas are earning a lot of money for the AAI, they
 should be given enough space to display their items.  The Committee desires that number of duty free shops should be
 increased and these shops should also have items of Indian handicrafts.  The Committee feels that at Indian airports
 there is a lot of potential to generate revenue from non-aeronautical sources and that a conscious effort should be made
 towards increasing the share of commercial revenue by fully exploiting the commercial potential of the airports.
 
CIVIC AMENITIES AT THE AIRPORTS
It has come to the notice of the Committee that there is utter lack of civic amenities like toilets, drinking water etc. at the
 airports.  The cleanliness and hygienic conditions of these places are not up to the mark and these are not being
 maintained properly.  It is noted that the officials working at the airports also use the same toilets, which are meant for
 the passengers/tourist.  The Committee was also informed that the toilet facilities are not available outside the
 arrival/departure halls of the airports.  Persons who come to receive/see off their clients/guests experience difficulty due
 to the absence of toilets outside the arrival/departure lounge.  Lack of toilet facility at car/taxi parking area outside the
 Airports also creates inconvenience.  Drivers are using the open space for toilet purpose as a result of which the whole
 parking area stinks. The Committee, therefore, recommends that there should be separate toilets for the officials
 working at the airports.  The Committee also recommends that toilet facilities are also to be provided outside the
 arrival/departure lounge and parking areas in order to avoid inconvenience to the persons who visit the airports to
 receive/see off their near and dear ones.  There should always be one or two persons on duty for proper cleaning of
 these places and regular inspection of these areas should be carried out for their proper maintenance.
 
TOUT PROBLEM

 conduct surprise checks on a daily basis.  The Committee further recommends that like Railways, which have their own
 Railways Protection Force, AAI can also have their own airport protection force to look into this problem.

 the foreign tourists have to travel very long distances to obtain visas to visit India.  Distance has acted as a disincentive
 to visit India.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should explore the possibility of
 introducing the facility of granting visa to visiting foreign tourists on arrival at the International Airports.

Many relatives/friends come to the airports to see off/receive their near and dear one, which creates congestion at the
 airport.  It has come to the notice of the Committee that most of the airports lack facility relating to the meeting and
 greeting place where people could meet a person to whom they have come to receive and see off.  It has also come to
 the notice of the Committee that passengers remain unaware of the friends/relatives who have come to the airport to
 meet and receive them.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Airports Authority of India should create meeting
 and greeting area facility at all the airports where people can receive and see off their friends/relatives.  In addition to a
 computerised information centre, facility for a message desk should also be provided at the airports so that the
 incoming passengers get the information that somebody is waiting for them.

A passenger can have some problems at the airport regarding visa, custom or requires some information related to delay
 flights etc., for which they look here and there. The Committee noted during discussion that such counters are not

 ‘May I Help You’ counters round the clock and an official should be present at these counters.  It would certainly give
 the impression that this country is welcoming the passengers/tourists.

 airports or remain inoperational over a considerable period due to lack of adequate maintenance facilities.   Therefore,

 Authority of India should give preference to build aerobridges at all the major airports in the country.  Wherever the
 aerobridges are lying dysfunctional, they should be made operational and put to use.

 aid facility to be used in case of need.  The Committee understands that there have been cases of death at the airports
 due to the absence of medical facilities.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that medical aid counters/chemists
 shops should be made available at all the airports where passengers can be treated in case of emergency and buy

 trolleys.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that AAI should look into the matter of providing sufficient number of
 spacious luggage trolleys.

        Tourism is not only a major social  phenomenon of the modern society with enormous economic
 consequences but also  the world’s largest export industry, which accounts for about 8% of the total
 world’s exports, more than 30% of international trade in services, 10.7% of the  global work force and
 about 12% of world GDP.   It is also dubbed as the ‘Largest Smokeless Industry’ and contributes
 towards preservation of clean environment.
 2.Tourism is presently India’s second  largest net foreign exchange earning export industry after
 textiles/garments.  The estimated foreign exchange earning during January to December 99 were
 $2916.01 millions as compared to $2819.62 millions during the same period of  1998 showing an
 increase of 3.4%. Foreign tourist arrival has gone upto 2471848  during 1999 registering a growth of
 4.8% as compared to 1998.
 3.Tourism is of a particular significance  so far as India is concerned since it contributes to the
 environment and to the  national integration as it helps in the interaction amongst social and cultural
 lives of the people.   Over 160 million domestic  tourists visiting different parts of the country every
 year return with a  better understanding of the people living in the other regions of the country  and the
 cultural diversity of India.
 4.Tourism not only has the capacity to  generate large-scale employment opportunities in remote and
 backward areas but  also provides employment to a large number of women, both educated and
 uneducated.   In fact women are employed  in a large number in hotels, airlines services, travel agencies,
 handicrafts making, cultural and other tourism-related activities.
 5.The Ministry of Tourism functions as the  nodal agency for development of tourism in the country by
 coordinating and  supplementing the efforts of the State/Union Territory Governments, catalysing
 private investment, strengthening promotional and market efforts and in  providing trained manpower
 resources.
 6.The Ministry of Tourism has under its administrative control the following public sector
 undertaking/autonomous bodies:-
a)  India Tourism Development Corporation Limited;
b) National Council for Hotel Management and Catering  Technology;
 c) Indian Institute of Tourism & Travel Management;
d) Institutes of Hotel Management, Catering Technology and  Applied Nutrition at different locations in
 the country;
e)  Food Craft Institutes at different locations;
f)   Indian Institute of Skiing & Mountaineering;
g) National Institute of Water Sports.
 7.In  addition to the Head-quarters Organisation at New Delhi, the Directorate  General of Tourism has
 21 tourism offices in India and 18 tourist offices overseas.
 8. Demand No.82, containing the details of  budget allocations of Ministry of Tourism for the financial
 year 2000-2001, was considered by the Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
 Transport & Tourism at its meeting held on the 23rd March 2000.
 9. The details of the plan allocations approved for the Ministry of Tourism for the last four years of the

10.     From a perusal of the Demands for Grants of  the Ministry of Tourism for 2000-2001, the
 Committee found that plan outlay of  the Ministry for the year 1999-2000 had been reduced from
 Rs.160.50 crores to  Rs.110 crores at RE stage.   Also the  plan outlay for the year 2000-2001 has been
 kept at Rs.135.00 crores which is less by Rs.24.50 crores as compared to BE for the year 1999-2000.
 11.     On being asked about the reasons for  reduction of plan outlay for 1999-2000 at RE stage and
 lower BE for the year  2000-2001, the Ministry of Tourism have stated that due to resource  constraints,
 not only BE 1999-2000 has been reduced but also proposed budget  allocation for the year 2000-2001
 has been subjected to drastic cut and the  Planning Commission has approved allocation of Rs.135.00
 crores only. The  Government    has neither been able to  enhance its own investment in the tourism
 sector nor mobilise private  investment to the desired extent due to the capital structure of industry,
 longer gestation period, low rates of return and certain infrastructural and  procedural problems.
 12.    The Committee has been  consistently recommending not to reduce the plan outlay of the Ministry
 at RE  stage. Moreover, while examining the Demands for Grants 1999-2000, the Committee  in its 37th
 Report had specially recommended a proportionate or at  least 20% increase over the previous year’s
 budget allocations.   However, to the surprise of the Committee,  plan outlay of Rs.135 crores has been
 approved for the year 2000-2001 against  the BE of Rs.160.5 crores for the last year.
 13.    The  Committee further observed that out of Rs.135.00 crores for the year 2000-2001,  Rs.49.75
 crores have been allocated for overseas campaign, thereby leaving only  Rs.85.25 crores for Human
 Resource Development, Tourist Infrastructure and  Domestic Campaign etc. in the country.
 14.         Tourism has a huge potential of employment opportunity in  rural and backward areas without
 causing migration to distant places, foreign  exchange earning industry, a tool for sustainable human
 development including  poverty alleviation, environmental conservation and regeneration, job creation
 and advancement of women and other disadvantaged groups.
 15.    The  Committee, therefore, again recommends that adequate funds be made available to  the
 Ministry of Tourism and there should be no reduction in the plan outlay at  RE stage.   The
 Committee is of the view that an amount Rs.85.25 crores is not sufficient to meet the requirement
 for  Domestic Campaign, Tourist Infrastructure, Training (Human Resource  Development) and
 other Expenditure and recommends that it should be increased at RE stage.
16.    The Committee is also concerned to note  that the Government policy has so far not been able to
 attract the private  investment in tourism sector to the desired extent.   The Committee is of the view that
 the Government alone, through  its limited resources, will not be able to meet the requirements of funds
 for  proper development of tourism sector.   The Committee, therefore, further  recommends that the
 Government, while acting as a facilitator and coordinator  and encouraging involvement of private
 sector in the development of tourism,  should take steps to remove the infrastructural and
 procedural hurdles which the private sector has to face and ensure the availability of land,
 electricity, water supply, sewerage system and do away with the multiplicity of  permits and
 approvals.
17.    The Committee notes that as against the  proposed outlay of Rs.5370 for the 9th Plan Period, only a
 minuscule  amount of Rs.485.75 crores was approved.   The Committee also notes that the Ministry of
 Tourism has so far been  allocated Rs.455.46 crores out of the total plan outlay of Rs.485.75 for the
 entire 9th Five Year Plan period. Now about Rs.30.29 crores remain  for the last financial year of the
 9th Plan Period i.e.  2001-2002.   The Committee feels that  this amount of Rs.30.29 crores would not be
 sufficient for the implementation  of various schemes already under consideration of the Ministry of
 Tourism.   The  Committee, therefore, recommends for substantial enhancement of the Plan Outlay
 of the Ministry of Tourism for the year 2001-2002 and that Planning Commission and Ministry of
 Finance should intimate the Ministry of Tourism about the  quantum of plan outlay well in
 advance, so that Ministry of Tourism may be able  to project its demands properly for the year
 2001-2002.  
CENTRAL ASSISTANCE FOR  TOURISM INFRASTRUCTURE & PRODUCT DEVELOPMENT  
18.     Since most of the tourist attractions and delivery systems are  within the purview of State/UT
 Governments, a large part of the Central  Government investment for the improvement and creation of
 tourist facilities is channelised through the State Governments on a cost-sharing basis.   In order to
 ensure integrated development of  tourism infrastructure including basic amenities and other facilities,
 the  Ministry of Tourism provides assistance to State/Union Territory Governments for the
 implementation of composite projects.   A total amount of Rs.29.10 crores has been allocated under this
 Head which  includes Rs.18 crores for integrated development of Tourist/Pilgrim Centres,  Special

 Tourism Areas, Major Tourism Projects, setting up of Paryatan Bhawan  etc., Rs.6.75 crores for
 development of facilities for domestic tourists such  as Budget Accommodation, Wayside Facilities etc.,
 Rs.4.10 crores for Product  Development such as refurbishment of monuments, Sound and Light
 Shows/Flood  Lighting, Adventure Tourism etc. and Rs.25 lakh for Externally Aided Projects.
 19.Central assistance for infrastructure development is provided  to the States based on two types of
 funding patterns – (1) Normal Funding and  (2) Equity Scheme.   The most popular  pattern of funding,
 which has been continuing over successive plan periods, is the normal funding. The Ministry of
 Tourism almost meets the entire expenditure  except the cost of land and interior decoration in the
 construction  projects.   A new method of funding,  namely ‘Equity Scheme’, had been introduced during
 1992-93 in which the  assistance from the Ministry of Tourism is limited to 28% of the project  cost.  
 12% of the project cost is to be  provided by the State Government/Union Territory and the balance 60%
 has to be  raised as loan from financial institutions/banks.   This method of funding is applicable to
 bankable projects requiring large investments.

 22.     The Committee had, in its 37th report on the Demands for Grants (1999-2000) of the Ministry of
 Tourism, identified the condition of  transferring the title of the land from State Government to the
 Government of  India as one of the major bottlenecks resulting in delay in the completion of  projects
 and had recommended the waiving off of this condition for development  of tourism in the country.   The
 Ministry  has informed that the Ministry of Urban Affairs & Employment, and also  Planning
 Commission, have supported the waiving of the condition of  transferring the title of land to
 Government of India.   The Ministry of Finance, however, has agreed  to substitute the condition of
 transfer of land by long-term lease.   However, many States have expressed their  reservation even on
 this requirement.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that  the matter may be taken up with
 the concerned State Government and the Ministry  of Finance to sort it out expeditiously so as to
 arrive at an amicable solution and the funds earmarked for implementation of various projects
 under this scheme are fully utilised without any further delay.  
23.      The Committee was also  informed that the State Governments are reluctant to approach Ministry
 of  Tourism for funds under the Equity Scheme since they have to share 12% of the  project cost and
 have also to obtain funds from financial institutions on loan  basis.   The Committee feels that the
 scheme is not bearing the desired fruits since it has not been able to encourage the participation
 of the States.   The Committee, therefore, recommends that in view of the indifferent attitude of
 the States, the viability of the scheme may  be reassessed since it is leading to non-utilisation of
 funds every year.   The Government should also try to modify the  scheme, in consultation with the
 State Governments, so that it becomes more  acceptable to the States and encourage their
 participation in this centrally  assisted financial scheme.

 Bhawan in Delhi for which 10870 sq. meters of land  has been allotted by the Ministry of Urban

 report for Bharat Paryatan Bhawan may be  completed soon so that the work for the actual
 construction may begin at the  earliest.  
WAYSIDE AMENITIES
25.     The Ministry of Tourism allocates funds every year to the State  Governments for creating wayside
 amenities for tourists.   These include tourist reception centres,  restaurants/cafeterias, drinking water
 facilities, public conveniences, kiosks,  general store and parking area etc. The Ministry of Tourism
 prioritises projects in consultation with the State Governments and release funds on  receipt of the
 specific proposals prioritised during the financial year.   An amount of Rs.4.00 crores has been
 allocated for the purpose during the year 2000-2001.
 26.    The  Committee feels that to keep pace with the fast developing highway tourism in the
 country, a well-knit network of wayside facilities on the roads connecting  important tourist
 centres is a must.   The Committee also feels that the allocation of Rs. 4 crores for wayside
 amenities in the BE 2000-2001 is simply not enough and recommends that the  allocation under
 this head must be increased.   The Government should also explore the possibility of involving the
 participation of private parties/voluntary agencies for the maintenance of  toilet/drinking water
 facilities and other civic amenities created under this scheme.  
PILGRIM TOURISM
27.     The Committee has been informed that for the development of  infrastructure facilities including
 basic amenities in the identified  tourist/pilgrim centres, the Ministry of Tourism has decided to provide
 financial assistance to the State/Union Territory Governments for the  implementation of composite
 projects in 50 selected centres.   The maximum assistance will be Rupees one  cores, subject to matching
 contribution by the State Governments, and it will  be provided at the rate of Rs.50 lakh for a period of
 two years.   The Ministry of Tourism has decided to set  up a ‘Pilgrim Tourism Development Board’ to
 advise the Ministry in all matters relating to Pilgrim Tourism.
28.    The  Committee is of the view that in India, there are a large number of pilgrim centres and if
 basic amenities/facilities are provided to the tourists/pilgrims, it  will encourage the arrival of the
 tourists at these places.   The Committee recommends that the ‘Pilgrim  Tourism Development
 Board’ may be set up immediately and the State Governments may be requested to provide the
 matching financial contributions so that  development work may take place at the selected tourist
 centres in their States on priority basis.        
MEGA-TOURISM PROJECTS/SPECIAL TOURISM AREAS 
29.     Mega Tourism  projects have brought revolution in tourism sector in Maxico and Indonesia and
 tourist arrivals have gone up substantially there.   In India an ambitious scheme for identification and
 development  of ‘Special Tourism Areas’, also known as “Mega Tourism Projects”, was taken up  during
 Eighth Plan period.   The State  Governments of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Orissa and Maharashtra and Union
 Territory  Administration of Daman and Diu declared Bekal Beach (Kerala), Puri-Konark Area  (Orissa),
 Sindhudurg (Maharashtra), Muttukadu-Mamallapuram (Tamil Nadu) and Diu  as Special Tourism Area
 for integrated development.   The intensive development of these areas was envisaged in  coordination
 with the concerned State Governments and private sector.   The Ministry of Tourism has proposed an
