 programmes, the indigenous R&D organisations have made significant achievement and contribution in solving road
 engineering problems such as introduction of new materials like rubber/polymer modified bitumen, use of fly ash in
 road construction and anti-corrosive techniques, road user cost study to access effect of road condition on vehicle
 operating cost, pavement deterioration models, aesthetical and environment friendly road side furniture, reinforced
 earth technology, development of computer software for analysis and design of highway bridge superstructure,
 instrumentation of simply supported bridges and cantilever bridges.  These organisations generally make their best of
 efforts to produce results commensurate with the investment made in the Research Schemes.  But due to indigenously
 non-availability of modern equipments & instruments, inadequate interaction between Indian and International
 technical/scientific community and lack of adequate fiscal incentives to promote R & D efforts in highway sector; the
 indigenous research and development could not be made at par with international levels.  At present there are 39
 ongoing schemes on R &D.   
53.       The Committee is not satisfied with the pace of development in the    Research & Development activities in the
 Road sector.  Till date, the indigenous Research & Development is not able to match the international level.  The
 Committee understands that the Ministry earlier facing the problem of shortage of funds.  However, now the Ministry is
 well satisfied with the availability of funds and hopes that the Ministry will now concentrate upon R&D activities on
 road sector and provide sufficient funds therefor. 
 
* * * * * * 
 
OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
HIGHER ALLOCATION FOR ROAD SECTOR
 
The Committee is happy to note that since 2000-2001 the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways has been getting
 sufficient funds as a result of which Ministry is now in a position to achieve the physical targets as initially envisaged
 for the Ninth Plan.  Earlier the Ministry has not been to exploit its potential due to paucity of funds.  Now there is no
 dearth of money for Road sector and so it is the turn of the Ministry to establish its expertise in the field of Road Sector.
(Para 12)
 
CENRTAL ROAD FUND 
The Committee is happy to note that with the setting up of the Central Road Fund, the Ministry of Road Transport &
 Highways has now been able to provide sufficient funds for the development and maintenance of State Highways and
 State Roads.  However, during the last year only an amount of Rs. 314.75 crores out of Rs.990 crores could be released
 to States for the purpose.  The Committee can understand this fact that within a short span of time, the States could not
 have been able to utilise whole amount of Rs. 990 crore allocated for the development of State Highways and State
 Roads.  The Committee hopes that in future the State Governments will be able to utilise the whole amount allocated to
 them in this regard.  However, the Committee wants the Ministry to impress upon the State Government that the State
 Highways and State roads should be developed in such a way that the entire State roads network would provide a feeder

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/51streport.htm[28-08-2018 12:52:11]
 system to the rail network thereby avoiding development of parallel road network.  The Committee is aware that there
 have been instances of diversion of funds and are not utilised for the purpose for which they are allocated. Therefore,
 Committee recommends that Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should ensure proper and strict monitoring of
 the schemes for which the funds are allocated from the Central Road Funds so as to avoid cost escalation and time over
 run.
(Para 16)
 
CHECK POINTS & SPEED BREAKERS AT NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
 
The Committee is of the view that the check points on National Highways are illegal collection points for the local
 police and local bodies where traffic is stopped and harassed.  The Committee is also of the view that speed breakers on
 the National Highways are one of the reasons for accidents.  Therefore, it is much needed to remove all these speed
 breakers from National Highways.  The Committee is unable to understand why State Governments have not complied
 and implemented the directions of the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways in this regard.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that the Ministry should impose some financial penalty on those states who violate the
 guidelines and fail to remove check points and speed breakers from National Highways.
(Para 20) 
 
EXCISE DUTY ON MIXING OF CEMENT
 
The Committee agrees to the view put forth by the Ministry that proposed excise duty on mixing of cement is likely to
 increase the cost of construction of National Highways and open the new way of the harassment.  The Committee is
 unable to understand as to what has made the Ministry of Finance to treat the mixing of cement as production activity. 
 The Committee is of the view that Central Excise Department is finding new ways and means to earn revenue and to
 impose excise duties. The mixing of cement is one of such the examples.  The Committee therefore recommends that
 the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should take up the matter strongly with Ministry of Finance (Department
 of Revenue) to review the proposal.
(Para 22)
 
DEVELOPMENT OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS IN NORTH EASTERN REGION
 
The Committee appreciates the steps taken by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways for development and
 improvement in the poor condition of the National Highways in the North East region.  The Committee hopes that
 allocated amount of Rs.282.15 crores will be fully utilised by the North Eastern States with the help of direct payment
 system as introduced by the Ministry. The Committee, however recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport and
 Highways should frame some schemes for this region which will help the contractors or Public Works Departments of
 these states to procure hot mix plants, boilers and any other related thing which is needed in the construction of roads. 
                                                                                                                                                                (Para 25)
 
GUIDELINES FOR DECLEARING NEW NATIONAL HIGHWAYS
 
The Committee notes that the Ministry of Road Transport &Highways  has been declaring State roads as National
 Highways in violation of the guidelines prescribed in this regard, frequently.  It has increased the burden of the
 Government for maintenance of National Highways.  The Committee therefore recommends that the guidelines issued
 in this respect should be adhered to strictly.  The problems relating to the transferring of land to the Centre,
 rehabilitation and relocation in the case of road widening and four laning of National Highway, should be taken care of
 well in advance and if possible, it should be the part of the guidelines.  The Committee hopes that this will check the
 delays in execution of plans for development of newly declared National Highways.
(Para 32)
ROAD SAFETY
 
The Committee is worried about the number of road accidents in the country.  The Committee is of the view that most
 of the accidents occurs due to the driver’s negligence, unawareness of the road safety norms and non-implementation of
 the Rules and Regulations.  The efforts made for reducing the road accidents are not sufficient enough to reduce the

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/51streport.htm[28-08-2018 12:52:11]
 number of road accidents.  
The Committee thinks that refresher training programme for heavy vehicle drivers in the non-organised sector has not
 achieved the desired results.  The Ministry should not feel satisfied that the number of road accidents are decreasing as
 compare to previous year. However, they should make efforts to further decrease the number of road accidents that are
 taking lives of thousand of people every year.  Traffic sense in general is missing among the drivers.  Human aspects
 should be made important component for the training programme of drivers. The Committee recommends that drivers
 should be educated with regard to road safety rules and regulations, which will decrease the number of accidents. 
The Committee appreciates the introduction of ‘Smart Card’ by the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways. The
 concept of smart card is an innovative step and will definitely minimise the cases of issuance of fake licenses.
(Paras 38, 39 and 40)
 
GRANTS-IN-AID TO NON GOVERNMENT ORGANISATIONS
 
The Committee is surprised to note that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways does not have their own
 monitoring system to see how the Grants-in-aid given to Non-Government Organisation to undertake various types of
 road safety programmes are utilised.    The Committee is of the view that in the absence of proper monitoring system,
 funds are likely to be misused.  There is a possibility of the fake Non Government Organisation who can come forward
 to obtain grants with the purpose to undertake road safety programmes.  
The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should set up its own
 monitoring system and should ensure that the grants, which have been allocated to Non Government Organisations,
 should be utilised for the purpose for which it is approved. The Ministry should also release the State-wise list of NGOs
 with their addresses for the information of general public. This will definitely increase the awareness of the public
 about the activities of Non Government Organisation which in turn will ensure proper utilisation of the allocated funds
 and reduce the chances of the corruption.
(Paras 44 and 45)
VEHICULAR POLLUTION
 
The Committee is not satisfied with the measures taken by the Ministry of Road Transport & Highways to check and
 control the pollution of the vehicles.  Thanks to the vehicular pollution, Delhi is known as one of the most polluted city
 in the world.  The Committee hopes that with the enforcement of use of CNG in public vehicle will reduce the level of
 vehicular pollution in Delhi and similar steps will be taken in respect of other polluted cities of the country. The
 Committee however recommends that Ministry of Road Transport and Highways should take up the matter of having
 more and more outlets in the country to provide CNG to vehicles to avoid wastage of time in standing in the long
 queues.
 
The Committee is aware of the fact that vehicle owners have to pay heavy charges for obtaining ‘Pollution under control
 Certificate’ for their vehicles. This has been proving as discouraging factor and public in general is less enthusiastic for
 having pollution check up of their vehicles.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Road
 Transport and Highways should take up the matter with the concerned agencies to create an environment where the
 vehicle owners may offer voluntarily first for testing their vehicles.
(Paras 48 and 49)
 
RESEARCH AND DEVELOPMENT ACTIVITIES
 
The Committee is not satisfied with the pace of development in the    Research & Development activities in the Road
 sector.  Till date, the indigenous Research & Development is not able to match the international level.  The Committee
 understands that the Ministry earlier facing the problem of shortage of funds.  However, now the Ministry is well
 satisfied with the availability of funds and hopes that the Ministry will now concentrate upon R&D activities on road
 sector and provide sufficient funds therefor.
(Para 53)

CONSTRUCTION OF SINGLE BUOY MOORING (SBM)
 
23.       The Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Transport and Tourism under took the study
 visit to Cochin and came to know the peculiar problem being faced by Cochin Port Trust by construction of Single
 Buoy Mooring (SBM).  In this connection the Committee held discussion with representatives of Cochin Port Trust and
 Kochi Refineries Ltd. 
24.       In his deposition before the Committee during the discussion, the representative of Kochi Refineries Ltd.
 informed that the present crude oil processing capacity of KRL is 7.5 million tonnes per annum.  The crude oil is
 received in tankers at specially constructed jetties in Cochin Port Trust and pumped to the Refineries’ Storage tanks
 through pipelines.  Since March 1998, Administered Pricing Mechanism (APM) was in force and the cost incurred by
 the Refineries in receiving crude oil and processing it into products was reimbursed completely by the Oil Co-
ordination Committee (OCC).  Since April 1998, the APM has been dismantled and the entire cost has to be borne by

REPORT
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/52ndreport.htm[28-08-2018 12:52:11]
 individual Refineries.  In this de-regulated scenario, KRL has to face competition from Private Sector Refineries in
 India as well as for imports, it was proposed to expand the crude oil processing capacity to 13.5 million tonnes per
 annum, along with measures to achieve value addition and cost reduction.  The present transportation cost of crude oil
 which contributes more than 50% of the total operating cost excluding the cost of crude oil, was identified as the most
 important area for cost reduction.  The only way to reduce cost was to receive crude oil in large ships.  However,
 Cochin Port, being an inland Port, has limitations for receiving large oil tankers.  It was in this background KRL
 thought of setting up an off-shore (i.e. 12 kms. away from the sea-shore and 6 kms. away from the Port limits) Single
 Buoy Mooring (SBM) and connected facilities which would be the cheapest option for operating the Refineries even at
 the existing level of 7.5 million tonnes.  
25.       The Committee also heard the views of the representative of the Cochin Port Trust after the presentation of the
 Representatives of Kochi Refinery Ltd. on the crucial problem faced by Cochin Port Trust.  The Committee was
 informed that in the event of setting up of the SBM by the KRL in the open sea, there would be non-utilisation of the
 existing infrastructure created by the port exclusively for the Kochi Refineries Ltd. (KRL) for handling POL products
 for their Refineries. 
26.       Cochin Port Trust developed two tanker berths way back in the 1950’s.  The Port Trust also developed an
 exclusive Oil Terminal in 1984 for handling POL products for KRL.  Other allied infrastructure such as flotilla, fire
 float, fire fighting facilities and also especially skilled manpower was created by the Port Trust exclusively for the
 Refinery.  The channel, which was 9.75 meters depth, was also dredged to 12.9 meters for handling bigger size vessels
 with a draft of 11.7 meters at Cochin Oil Terminal, by expending around Rs. 50 crores.  The total investment on the
 entire infrastructure created for the KRL would come to Rs. 100 crores.  The present move of KRL will make the entire
 Port infrastructure created exclusively for the KRL infructuous.   Once the POL handling operations are shifted to the
 proposed SBM, it will jeopardise the very survival of the Port.  The Port has already suggested to KRL that the Port
 Trust is prepared to create additional infrastructure for handling crude oil products. 
27.       The Committee wanted to know as to why the KRL did not take the Cochin Port Trust into confidence before
 going ahead with setting up of the SBM Project, especially, when the Port Trust was serving the KRL for the last so
 many years for handling POL products for the Refineries.  The Committee wanted to know the action taken by the
 Cochin Port Trust on their part after knowing about setting up of the SBM Project by KRL. 
28.       In reply, the Committee was informed by the KRL representative that the service being provided by the Cochin
 Port Trust was not considered economical in the de-regulated scenario.  Moreover, once the SBM was set up, there
 would not be any recurring loss to KRL, and the Consultant appointed to make feasibility study for the purpose opined
 that the project should be taken up at the earliest for implementation.  Any delay in its implementation would entail cost
 escalation.  So they decided to go ahead with the project independently.  It was also felt that consulting another
 organisation might delay the process.  It was mentioned that the mechanical completion of the project would take 36
 months and after that another three months for commissioning.  The Environmental Clearance for KRL’s Capacity
 Expansion Project including the crude oil receipt facilities had been obtained from the Ministry of Environment &
 Forests.  KRL is against any alternative proposal which would attract recurring expenditure on account of dredging etc. 
 Any delay in timely completion of the Project will entail cost escalation by about 25% of the total estimate.  The
 Planning Commission is also vehemently against any delay in commissioning the Project. 
29.       While clarifying the points raised by the KRL, the representative of Cochin Port Trust Stated that despite
 repeated requests by Cochin Port Trust,  KRL was extremely reluctant to share any information about their plans of
 expansion including the setting up of the SBM.  However, based on information having obtained from informal sources
 about the SBM, Cochin Port Trust immediately made representation to the Ministry of Surface Transport and the

CUSTOMS RELATED DIFFICULTIES FACED BY USER AGENCIES WORKING AT THE PORTS 
 
33.       The Committee also came to know about the Custom related problems being faced by various using agencies
 working at the Ports which in turn affecting the functioning of the Ports.   In this connection Committee during its visits
 to Cochin had the opportunity to acquaint itself to situation particularly at the Cochin Port Trust and held discussion
 with the concerned agencies.  The details of the some of the problems, which were brought to notice of the Committee,
 have been given in succeeding paragraphs.   
(i)         Issue of passes to main line operators. 
34.       The representative of the Cochin Steamer Agent’s Association Stated that the Customs do not recognize the
 Main Line Operators (MLOs) as Steamer Agents as far as containerized cargo is concerned and insist for
 filling/amendment of manifests by feeder line operators only.  If one MLO delays the submission of the Imports
 manifest of one container to the feeder line operator, the filling of the entire vessel’s containers manifest would be
 delayed resulting in delay for onward movement of containers like ICD, House De-stuffing, CFS movements etc.  In
 fact, the custodian of the cargo is the MLO.  It was stated that mammoth carriers, viz. Evergreen, Mearsk, German
 Express etc are not in a position to call directly at the Port and they can only operate through feeder lines.  In the
 circumstance, it may be considered to recognise the MLOs as Steamer Agents to amend/file manifest separately for
 each of their container, which would save a lot of time in clearance of Cargo/containers and consequential financial loss
 to the trade. 
35.       The representative of Customs Cochin clarified that as per the Customs Act, 1962, the transaction i.e.
 entry/departure/clearance/loading and unloading of the cargo in the Customs area has to be performed by the Master of
 the vessel or his authorised Agents.  As per the Act, the responsibility to account for the cargo carried by the vessel
 rests on the Master of the vessel.  If the cargo is not satisfactorily accounted for, the Master of the vessel is liable for
 penal action.  The Act, hence does not recognise Main Line Operators or feeder line operators, and expects the Master
 of the vessel to be responsible for the cargo carried by him.  Hence manifest filed by the Master of the vessel cannot be
 amended by any person other than the authorised Steamer Agents without his concurrence.  As such, it would not be
 possible to permit either the MLOs or feeder line operators other than the authorised Steamer Agents from
 filing/amending the manifest as per the provisions of the Customs Act.  The Customs do not have any control or
 jurisdiction over the Main Line Operator who operates in a far off place.  The Customs has control only over the person
 who actually brings the cargo to the Port.   The Customs Act warrants proper accountability of the cargo being brought
 to India.  At present, the feeder line operator has to depend on the MLOs for all information’s relating to the cargo
 coming through containers, i.e. the feeder line operator need not always be aware of the contents of the container.  In
 the absence of proper accountability no one could be held responsible particularly so in case contraband goods,
 narcotics or explosives are carried in containers, even though Section 116 of he Customs Act envisages taking penal
 action against the person who brings unaccounted cargo to India.  In the circumstances, without amending the relevant
 provisions in the existed Customs Act, the Customs is not in position to issue passes to the MLOs.

UNIFORMITY IN PORTS TARIFF
 
43.       The Committee was informed that the regulation is considered essential wherever the provide of services
 factions in a monopoly or near monopoly situation.  The regulatory authority is considered necessary even when the
 monopoly service provides in the State. The Major Ports Trusts Act, 1963 was amended by Port Laws (Amendment)
 Act 1997 (15 of 1997) to provide for an independent Tariff Authority for Major Ports for fixing and revising the Port
 Tariff.  An independent authority i.e. tariff authority for Major Ports (TAMP) for the above purpose was set up on 10
th
 April, 1997.  TAMP has jurisdiction only on major port trusts which are administered under the Major Port Trusts Act
 1963. 
44.       Till very recently, Indian Ports faced no competition and in most cases lay down the law in their own without
 any fear of loosing customers and facing down turn in business.   Their main concern was how to reduce the time that
 ships spent outside the berths waiting for a chance to avail of their services.  However the developments of the last few
 years have changed all this drastically.  Where formerly ships had to wait for a chance to enter on over crowded Indian
 Port, they have new choices of using developing and fast coming new Ports i.e. Minor/State Ports. In the Mumbai itself,
 Mumbai Port, Jawaharlal Nehru Port, the privately owned and managed Pipavau Port or even the newly developed
 Mundra Port further north on the west coast.  Each of these Ports is competing with each other to woo customers by
 competitive tariffs and superior service. The traffic of minor Ports from 36 million tonnes in 1998-99 to about 80
 million tonnes this year and 100 MT approximately during 2001-02 is an important remarkable development in the port
 sector.
 
45.       The Committee is of the view that in the present age of liberlisation and decentarlisation of power, monopoly of
 the State is itself going out.  To boost the Indian business and make friendly competitive environment, there is need to
 eradicate red tapism, rules & regulations to the extent as to which it is possible.  In the present scenario, minor and
 State Ports are developing with the fast pace and challenging the status of the Major Ports.  Tariff authority for Major
 Ports which regularise only the tariff for the Major Ports does not have any authority /control over the tariff at minor
 and State Ports. This situation gives special benefit of lower tariff to Minor/State Ports as to attract comparatively more
 cargo. 
46.       It is not appreciable that while facing the new challenges, the Major Ports are to be regulated in case of port
 tariff by the extra statutory/constitutional authority.  Due to the regulation of port tariff of Major Ports, the level playing
 field between Major Ports and minor/State Ports does not exist since only Major Ports come under the jurisdiction of
 regulating authority while other Ports do not.  It is a clearly discrimination towards the Major Ports of the country.  The
 Committee therefore recommends that uniformity of tariff at Ports in the country is highly required among the major,
 minor and State Ports.  In the present scenario of modernisation and Corporatisation of Ports, it is very essential that our
 Major Ports should have liberty to fix port tariff at their own.  In such case, there is no need of regulatory authority over
 Ports i.e. Tariff authority for Major Ports.  The Ministry of Shipping should seriously analyse the situation and bring
 necessary legislation in this regard to ensure uniformity in the Tariff of all Ports in the country.

65.       The Committee was apprised that now a day Indian Shipping Sector is facing heavy taxation, which is
 obstructing its natural growth.  The Mudaliar Committee, constituted after independence to go into the question of
 recommendations on how to increase India’s Shipping strongly recommended that Independent India should have a
 strong merchant fleet.  Till 1975-76, Indian Shipping achieved the target of 5 MT.  After that it has not been able to
 achieve much increase in the rate of growth.  The Ninth Plan target is 9 MTs.  The Ministry is of the view that this
 target is hardly to achieve due to several reasons, which obstructs the growth of shipping sector. 
66.       The Committee further apprised that Indian Shipping Sector is yet to be provided a friendly and facilitator
 policy.  It is evident that the shipping industry does not grow with itself, as the automobile industry or any other
 industry.  Where there are a number of indigenous companies, which compete with each other.  Where as in India’s
 Shipping Sector all major concerns i.e. Shipping Corporation of India, Great Eastern or Chougule do not compete each
 other in the Indian market.  They compete with international market.  This type of situation is not favourable to India’s
 Shipping Sector. 
67.       The Committee also came to know that shipping fleets of the most of the countries are enjoying benefits of zero-
tax regimes i.e. Singapore, U.K. etc.  All of them introduced zero tax-regimes.  The rate of taxation is 1% at the most. 
 Whereas, in India, shipping sector have regular taxation, which costs from 35% to 38%.  Besides this, the five percent
 (5%) customs duty has also imposed on the import of ships, which has never been in the past.  There is no country in
 the international arena, which imposes tax on ships.  High rate of tax i.e. 25% on the interest payment of external

 will also definitely boost the traffic handling and increase the capacity of the Major Ports in the country.  The 9th plan
 working group had made a projection of traffic of 424 million tonnes by the end year of 9th Five Year Plan.  It is
 anticipated by the Ministry that traffic handling of Major Ports may be at the best reach to a level of 325 MT.  It is also
 assessed that the capacity addition during the 9th plan will be of the order of 157 MT. The Committee is unhappy on the
 failure of achievement of projected Cargo handling of 424 MT as projected by the 9th plan-working group.  During the
 year 2000-2001, the Ports have not been able to utilise their traffic handling capacity of 314 MT and only 283.80 MT of
 the traffic was handled during that year.  The Committee is also disappointed to note that against the capacity of 344
 MT the Ministry has projected traffic handling of 325 MT for this year.  The Committee hopes that the Major Ports will
 utilise the additional capacity to be created this year and will enhance their cargo handling efficiency.
(Paras 13 and 17)
 
DEVELOPMENT OF MINOR PORTS
The Committee appreciates the performance shown by these minor/captive Ports.  Minor Ports are serving as alternative
 of the Major Ports in some cases and minimising the extra burden on the Major Ports.  The Committee is happy to note
 that the Ministry of Shipping is giving attention to it and supporting the development of these Minor Ports.  The
 Committee is of the view that Major Ports of the country are in the process of Corporatisation and modernisation which
 will definitely enhance their Cargo handling efficiency.  There is a need to look after these minor Ports also.  Their
 modernisation is also much needed along with the modernisation of Major Ports. Minor Ports can play catalytic and
 proactive role in the development of Inland Water Transport System in the country.  The Committee, therefore,
 recommends that Ministry of Shipping should frame such schemes for technical/financial support to the respective
 maritime States for modernisation and development of these minor Ports, inspite of the fact that these are monitored
 and maintained by the States. 
(Para 22)

The Committee is of the view that there has been total lack of interaction between Kochi Refineries Ltd. and Cochin
 Port Trust in the matter of construction of Single Buoy Mooring which is likely to make the entire Port infrastructure

(Para 32)
 
CUSTOMS RELATED DIFFICULTIES FACED BY USER AGENCIES WORKING AT THE PORTS 
ISSUE OF PASSES TO MAIN LINE OPERATORS
 
The Committee is of the view that world over the cargo handling activities have undergone a lot of transformation.  If
 the Main Line Operators are allowed to file/amend the manifest treating them as Steamer Agents for their specific
 boxes, it will reduce the difficulties of Custom House Agents and also the duration of stay of imports loaded boxes at
 the Port.  The Committee feels that with the advancement of the containerization, there are multiple Steamer Agents for
 containers carried by a particular vessel and therefore recommends that the Main Line Operators should also be
 recognised as Steamer Agents. 
The Committee is also of the view that of late the definition of cargo has changed from a physical unit to one which
 assures responsibility.  World over container traffic has been growing in a fast pace.  In the changed scenario of
 containerization the responsibility of the cargo actually rests with the main line operators.  The Customs Act was
 enacted in 1962 at a time when the concept of containerization was not there.  Amendment to the existing custom is
 inevitable to cater the needs of the Custom House Agents.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that Ministry of
 Shipping should look into the matter and approach concerned Ministry of the Government of India for suitable
 amendment in the Custom Act 1962.
(Paras 36 and 37)
 
CUSTOMS OVERTIME BOOKINGS 
The Committee is surprised to see the present system of engaging the custom officials on payment of overtime
 individually and separately for custom clearance on Sundays/holidays and after office hours which perhaps may be
 against the existing financial principles.  The Committee is unable to understand that why every Agent/Shipper is
 insisted to pay overtime to the custom officials.  The Committee is of the opinion that in the era of containerization of
 Cargoes, it is not an appreciable practice and recommends that Port Trusts should be allowed to pay overtime payments
 to the custom officials in case they handle the work on Sundays/holiday and after office hour.  The Committee
 recommends that the Ministry of Shipping should take initiative in the matter and should approach the Ministry of
 Finance to settle the matter.                                                                          
(Para 40) 
 
AMENDMENTS ON ORDERS RELATING TO CUSTOMS REGULATIONS/NOTIFICATIONS
 
The Committee seriously notes the delay in processing the claims in accordance with the amended regulations.  The
 Committee is unable to understand that why clarifications on the orders relating to customs regulations/notifications
 issued by the Ministry of Finance are not treated as amendments and implemented with immediate effect in Cochin
 Port, where as, in other Major Ports these are treated as amended and implemented immediately.  The Committee,
 therefore, recommends that the Ministry of Shipping should take up the matter with the Ministry of Finance to resolve
 the issue/problem as early as possible to avoid delay in processing the claims at Ports in the country.
(Para 42)
 
UNIFORMITY IN PORTS TARIFF

The Committee is of the view that in the present age of liberlisation and decentarlisation of power, monopoly of the
 State is itself going out.  To boost the Indian business and make friendly competitive environment, there is need to
 eradicate red tapism, rules & regulations to the extent as to which it is possible.  In the present scenario, minor and
 State Ports are developing with the fast pace and challenging the status of the Major Ports.  Tariff authority for Major
 Ports which regularise only the tariff for the Major Ports does not have any authority /control over the tariff at minor
 and State Ports. This situation gives special benefit of lower tariff to Minor/State Ports as to attract comparatively more
 cargo. 
It is not appreciable that while facing the new challenges, the Major Ports are to be regulated in case of port tariff by the
 extra statutory/constitutional authority.  Due to the regulation of port tariff of Major Ports, the level playing field
 between Major Ports and minor/State Ports does not exist since only Major Ports come under the jurisdiction of
 regulating authority while other Ports do not.  It is a clearly discrimination towards the Major Ports of the country.  The
 Committee therefore recommends that uniformity of tariff at Ports in the country is highly required among the major,
 minor and State Ports.  In the present scenario of modernisation and Corporatisation of Ports, it is very essential that our
 Major Ports should have liberty to fix port tariff at their own.  In such case, there is no need of regulatory authority over
 Ports i.e. Tariff authority for Major Ports.  The Ministry of Shipping should seriously analyse the situation and bring
 necessary legislation in this regard to ensure uniformity in the Tariff of all Ports in the country.
(Para 45 and 46) 
 
INLAND WATER TRANSPORT
 
The Committee appreciates the measures taken by the Ministry of Shipping towards development and boosting of
 Inland Waterways Transport in the country.  Though the Committee feels that that why the Government has taken the
 initiative for the development of Inland Waterways too late. The major initiatives have come only in the last lag of the
 9
th Five Year Plan.  The Committee is of the view that one of the reasons for the slow pace of development of Inland
 Waterways is lack of co-ordination between State Governments and Central Government.  State Governments have not
 given due preference to this cheapest and unpolluted mode of Transport.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that
 the Ministry of Shipping should ensure proper co-ordination among the respective State Governments where Inland
 Waterways have been declared as National Waterways. 
The Committee is unhappy to note that the Ministry of Shipping has failed to utilise allocated funds, during 2000-2001,
 for the development of North Eastern Region and Sikkim.  The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry of
 Shipping should give proper attention to the North East Region and Sikkim in case of development of Inland Water
 Transport Sector and hope that the amount allocated for the current year will be fully utilised. 
The Committee is of the view that testing of the silt is required by the Major/Minor Ports and Inland Waterways Sector. 
 But this facility is available only at the Headquarter of the IWAI at Noida that delays the processing of samples.  The
 Committee, therefore, recommends that silt-testing facility should be decentralised and made available at various
 places/centres of the country.
(Paras 51, 53 and 55)
 
SHIPPING SECTOR
 
The Committee appreciates the efforts of the Government for creating an environment, which has ensured the
 participation of private sector in the field of training to cadet/officers in marine engineering and nautical discipline. 
 Particularly at a time when the Government is not in a position to provide enough funds for such facilities.  It has
 definitely opened the doors of employment opportunities in the Shipping Sector for the new generation.  The
 Committee is, however, worried about the prevailing unfair means/practices and discriminatory attitude adopted by
 these private training institutions and feels that the Ministry of Shipping has not taken enough steps to check the
 corruption, which is rampant in these training institutions.  The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of
 Shipping should ensure the frequent inspections of these training institutes so as to prohibit these institutions from
 indulging in unfair means and malpractices.  The Ministry should, if necessary, amend and make more stringent
 relevant rules regulating the functioning of   these institutes. The Ministry of Shipping should also take steps to keep a
 watch on the functioning of Seamen’s Employment Offices.

     The Aircraft (Exemption from Taxes and Duties on Fuel and Lubricants) Bill, 2000 seeks to exempt from
 payment of all customs duties, local duties, taxes, etc. on Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) and other items uplifted by an
 aircraft belonging to a foreign airline operating international service to, from and through India.
2.       The Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill states that bilateral air services agreements signed by the
 Government of India with other countries provide for, on reciprocal basis, either grant of outright exemption from
 payment of custom duties, local duties, taxes, etc., on Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) and other items uplifted by aircraft
 of one Contracting State from the territory of the other Contracting State or grant of most favoured nation treatment in
 these matters to the airlines of the Contracting States.
3.       The Bill has been introduced in order to fulfill the obligations arising out of the air services agreements and the
 Resolution of the International Civil Organization (ICAO).  The ICAO had adopted a resolution in December 1993,
 which, inter alia, provides that when an aircraft registered in one State or an aircraft leased or chartered by an operator
 of that State departs from an international airport of another State either for another customs territory of that latter State
 or for the territory of any other State, the fuel, lubricants and other consumable technical supplies taken on board for
 consumption during the flight shall be exempt from all customs and other duties.  Such duties and taxes shall include
 those levied by any taxing authority within a State, whether national or local.
4.       It is in pursuance of the fulfillment of the obligations arising out of the air services agreements and the resolution
 of the ICAO as detailed above, the Central Government was earlier paying subsidy to the State Governments for
 exempting the international airlines from levy of sales tax on ATF uplifted by them from India.  The Ministry of Civil
 Aviation in their background brief in respect of this Bill has pointed out that as a part of the general policy for reduction
 or elimination of various subsidies, the scheme was discontinued from the 1st December 1994 by the Central

 Government.
5.       The Ministry’s brief further states that following discontinuation of the subsidy by the Government,
 representations were received from foreign airlines stating that the levy of sales tax was contrary to the provisions of
 bilateral air agreement signed by the Government of India as well as the resolution adopted by the ICAO.  Keeping in
 mind the obligations arising out of the bilateral air services agreements and ICAO resolution, the present legislation has
 been proposed to be enacted under article 253 read with Entry 14 of List-I of the VII Schedule of the Constitution of
 India to exempt from all duties and taxes the fuel and lubricants uplifted by an aircraft registered in another State
 operating international services to, from and through India.
6.       The Ministry in its note has clarified that the new legislation will provide exemption from levy of sales tax on
 ATF and lubricants to foreign airlines only.  The exemption will not be available to national carriers as the legislation
 under article 253 can be resorted to only for the purpose of fulfilling obligations under international treaties. 
7.       In its meeting held on the 14th March 2001, the Committee had preliminary discussions on the provisions of the
 Bill.  It decided to obtain the suggestions/views of the domestic airlines operating in the country as also of the State
 Governments from where international flights are operating on the provisions of the Bill.
8.       In the light of the suggestions made by the domestic airlines and the State Governments concerned, the
 Committee heard the views of the representatives of the Ministry of Civil Aviation in its meeting held on the 7th
 August 2001.
VIEWS OF THE STATE GOVERNMENTS
9.       The Committee sought the views of the State Governments of Andhra Pradesh, Assam, Delhi, Karnataka,
 Maharashtra, Tamilnadu, West Bengal, Gujarat, Goa, Punjab and Kerala, the States which are likely to be affected by
 the provisions of the Bill.   Most of the State Governments have stated that they have no objection to the proposed Bill
 being passed by the Parliament of India.  However, they have added that the exemption of sales tax for the international
 airlines would result in substantial revenue loss to them and would have adverse effect on their finances.  The State
 Governments have, therefore, suggested that the loss as a result of this exemption may be made good by the
 Government of India by an annual grant equivalent to the loss of revenue suffered by the respective State Governments.
VIEWS OF THE DOMESTIC PRIVATE AIRLINES
10.     The Committee sought the views of the domestic private airlines operating in the country on the provisions of the
 Bill.  M/s Jet Airways and M/s Sahara Airlines have highlighted that the sales tax and other levies charged over and
 above the basic rate of fuel by the oil companies varies from 20 per cent to 30.55 per cent depending on the State
 Government.  These airlines have stated that this adds to the total cost of operations and have argued that this high levy
 of domestic duties is not at par with the matching revenue earning potential of the various sectors serviced by them.  
 The two airlines have, therefore, expressed hope that exemption given to the international carriers will be extended to
 the domestic airlines as well.
VIEWS OF THE MINISTRY OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS
11.     The Committee sought the views of the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas on the Bill with specific reference
 to the practice hitherto being followed of reimbursing the State Governments for the revenue loss which probably is
 met out of Oil Pool Fund. The Committee has been informed by the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas that after
 December, 1994, while the oil companies are depositing the due sales tax amounts with the State Government
 authorities, they are unable to recover this amount from the foreign airlines.   Thus, it is the oil companies and not the
 State Governments which are suffering revenue loss on this account.   As on March 31, 2001, the cumulative
 outstanding of the oil companies on account of under-recoveries due to sales tax on sales of ATF to the international
 airlines had reached a staggering figure of about Rs.694 crores.  The Ministry have pointed out that the oil companies
 cannot go on incurring this loss particularly in the post-administered-price-mechanism period.  The outstanding dues
 have adversely affected the liquidity of oil companies and these companies have been, time and again, raising this issue
 with the Central Government requesting for an early reimbursement of the outstanding amount.   The Ministry of
 Petroleum and Natural Gas have emphasized that not only the outstanding amounts need to be quickly reimbursed by
 the Government to the oil companies but also the proposed legislation should be enacted at the earliest so as to contain
 the future under-recoveries on this account.
12.     The pricing of ATF has been decontrolled with effect from 1.4.2001, and hence the prices of ATF are market-

 the foreign airlines could be loaded on to the selling price.   The oil companies have been assured that the under-
recoveries on this count after 1.4.2001 would be compensated from the oil pool account till such time the proposed

14.     In the Committee’s meeting held on August 7, 2001, the Secretary, Civil Aviation made a presentation on the Bill

15.     The Secretary, Civil Aviation, was specifically asked as to whether a discussion was held with the concerned
 State Governments before introducing the Bill.  The Secretary, Civil Aviation, did not give a direct reply to this specific
 query and inter-alia stated "…… there are certain obligations when two Sovereign States enter into an agreement.   One
 of the obligations, as in this case, is that the duties are not paid.  This is the fundamental point I am making …..".  He
 also observed that the State Governments were not at all entitled to this subsidy which they have been enjoying.   With
 regard to as to how long this practice of reimbursement by the Central Government to the State Governments had been
 going on, the Secretary, Ministry of Civil Aviation, stated that it might be around forty years.  The Committee had
 asked the Ministry of Civil Aviation as to whether there was any proposal to extend the benefit of sales tax exemption
 to Air India and other domestic airlines.  The Committee was informed that a separate proposal was being considered to
 exempt Indian carriers going abroad from exemption of sales tax by declaring upliftment of ATF as deemed exports. 
 However, this facility will not be available to domestic carriers operating within the country.
16.     The Committee also enquired from the Ministry of Civil Aviation regarding the criterion/rate of sales tax being
 charged by various States on ATF and whether the criterion was the same for the domestic and international airlines.
 The Ministry of Civil Aviation informed the Committee that the criteria for charging sales tax on ATF by various States
 is a state matter.  The criteria being adopted by the states for sales tax on domestic and international airlines as well as

CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATIONS
17.     The Committee is of the view that the passage of this legislation is no doubt essential in order to fulfill the
 international obligations and bilateral treaties entered into with foreign countries.  However, at the same time, it feels
 that the State Governments have for almost forty years been provided with a facility, namely, reimbursement of sales
 tax by the Central Government and since December 1 1994, through the Oil Pool Fund.  The amount involved in each
 of the State concerned is fairly substantial.  Sudden stoppage of this source of income is bound to adversely affect their
 already precarious financial condition.   The Committee feels that the State Governments should have been consulted
 while enacting the legislation which directly concerns them, particularly in an important area such as financial matter. 
 The Committee recommends that the Central Government should continue to reimburse the State Governments of the
 loss of revenue which might result once this enactment is passed by the Parliament and comes into effect. 
18.     The Committee notes that a separate proposal is being considered by the Ministry of Civil Aviation to exempt
 domestic carriers going abroad from exemption of sales tax on ATF.  The Committee appreciates the proposal and
 hopes that the same would be implemented at the earliest.
19.     The Committee at its meeting held on October 29, 2001, took up clause-by-clause consideration of the Bill.   The
 Committee, having regard to the submission made by the representatives of the Ministry of Civil Aviation and
 documents made available to it on this subject, is of the opinion that there is a need to fulfill the international
 obligations and to achieve the objectives set out in the Statement of Objects and Reasons of the Bill.
20.     Clause II and III were adopted without any modification.
21.     The Committee notes that the proposed legislation is to exempt only the foreign carriers from the payment of

REPORT
Roads have traditionally been the principal mode of connectivity between places and in hilly areas; they are often the
 only mode available for the transportation of men and material. Apart from carrying traffic independently from point to
 point, our road system is the main feeder to the railway system, ports and harbours and thus forms a part of integrated
 transport network. The development and maintenance of the National Highways is the responsibility of the Central
 Government, which is normally carried out through the agency of the State Governments. The rest of the network i.e.
 State Highways, major District Roads and village roads is with the State Governments and Panchayat Raj Institutions.
 The Border Roads Organisation is entrusted with construction and maintenance of strategic roads in the hilly and
 difficult terrain areas.
2.         Protection of her borders is always an important task for any Nation in the World. Due to variation in
 geographical stature, the country like India has foremost and very important responsibility to guard her borders from
 the enemies. Roads near the borders i.e. border roads also play vital role in safeguarding the borders of the nation as
 they provide critical help to operational defence priorities.
3.         Keeping in view the importance of Border Roads Organisation, the Committee decided to make-an indepth-
study of functioning of the Border Roads Organisation. Giving the details of the evolution of the Border Roads
 Organisation, the Border roads Development Board in their brief stated that prior to independence, a general impression
 prevailed that the North and North East borders of the country were quite immune to any external aggression because
 of the mighty Himalayas. But the subsequent infiltration of armed insurgents in Kashmir in 1948 and the claim of
 China over Tibet generated an awakening in the psyche of the Indian leadership, that the Himalayas were no longer a
 reliable natural barrier against possible aggression from across the border. The early years of post independence era
 exposed India to 15000 kms long border needed to be protected. Intimately connected with it was the fate and future
 development of the vast, remote and economically backward North and North Eastern Region having a poor road
 communication network.
4.         With the Constitution having declared road development as a State subject, this responsibility continued in the
 North and North Eastern States to rest with the State PWDs even where the defence strategy and operations were
 involved. However, soon it emerged that the roads to the Border States were forbidding challenges, needing dedicated
 commitment, time and money. An overall slow progress saw critical operational defence priorities getting seriously
 delayed, over the first two Five Year Plans.
5.         It was, therefore, in 1960, that the need for a single executive body for road development in the remote north and
 North Eastern Region of the country was strongly felt. Thus, on 29
th March 1960, the Border Roads Development
 Board (BRDB), as an inter-ministerial body with the status of a department was set up, under the Chairmanship of the
 then Prime Minister, late Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru, to co-ordinate an economically viable plan for expeditious execution
 of roads and other development projects, aimed primarily at enhancing the defence potential and at the same time
 accelerating the economic development of the North and North Eastern Border States. The Director-General (Border
 Roads) (DGBR) is the field arm of the Border Roads Development Board (BRDB).
6.         The Border Roads Organisation (BRO) was set up on 7
th May 1960, as a road construction executive force,
 partly integral to and in support of the Army and primarily conceived to meet its strategic requirements. Headed by a
 Director General Border Roads (DGBR), as the Executive head, it provided a General Reserve Engineer Force (GREF),
 as the execution force, to build and maintain roads, through an establishment of Chief Engineer Projects. The GREF is
 a unique force, conceived as an unarmed, civilian Organisation as per Article 33 of the Constitution, but modeled and
 trained on military pattern. This civil force in uniform was subjected to the CCS (C&A) Rules 1965 and also to the
 provisions of the Army Act and Rules for discipline.

8.         With a humble beginning of just two projects-Project Tusker (renamed Project Vartak) in the East at Tezpur and
 Project Beacon in the West at Srinagar, the BRO grew within a short period of three years to seven Projects due to
 overwhelming response and result oriented functioning. Producing quality work with little time or cost overrun, even in
 the most adverse conditions of working is the hallmark of the BRO. Additional work, not only from the Army but also
 from other Central Government Ministries, State Government and Public Sector Undertakings got entrusted to the
 BRO. As a result, the BRO has grown further from strength to strength over the last four decades to become a vast and
 vibrant Organisation with thirteen Chief Engineer Projects spread across the length and breath of the country.
9.         Each project is headed by a Brigadier from the Corps of Engineers or a GREF officer of the rank of a Chief
 Engineer, a task force by a Colonel or a Superintending Engineer and functional platoons by a Captain or an Asst.
 Engineer.
10.       At present, the Border Roads Organisation employs approximately 70,000 casual paid labourers over and above
 33, 123 GREF personnel. Over the years, the Border Roads Organisation has diversified from road construction to
 flyovers, permanent bridges, and airfields, major building projects and in a modest way to allied works for
 hydroelectric and tunneling projects.
ROLE/FUNCTIONS OF THE BRODER ROADS ORGANISATION
The Government of India has laid down the role of Border Roads Organisation in times of peace and emergency/war i.e.
Role of Border Roads Organisation in Peace
To develop and maintain the operational road infrastructure of General Staff in the border areas.
To contribute to the socio–economic development of the border states.
Role of Border Roads Organisation in War
To develop and maintain roads to keep Line of Control through in original sectors and re-deployed sectors.
To execute additional task as laid down by the Government contributing to the war effort.
12.       During operations and emergencies, the BRO perform, apart from the basic-role of development/maintenance of
 roads, to keep the line of communication. The following tasks may be entrusted by the COAS/Army Commander: -
Construction/Maintenance of Advance landing Grounds, helipads and helidromes.
Handling of Stores in Advance maintenance Area, Corps Maintenance Area and Engineer stores dumps.
Construction of Bailey bridges.
DCB Filling Schemes, Flooding Schemes and repair/maintenance of canals.
To assist Engineers in construction of under ground command and control centres for formation Head Quarters.
13.       The works executed by the BRO are divided into two broad categories:-
General Staff Works- The works, which the BRO executes as per the requirements of the Military Operations
 Directorate of Army Headquarters (MO Dte), are called General Staff (GS) Works. These works are based on a ten-
year General Staff Road Perspective Plan finalised by the MO Dte, in consultation with Headquarter Commands. The

61.       The Committee is unhappy to note that the personnel of the Border Roads Organisation are being discriminated
 in case of compensation on death due to accident or hostilities. Therefore, the Committee recommends that
 compensation should be given to the families of the deceased BRO personnel at par with that given in the case of other
 Central Government Organisation/Departments and Government should also give priority to implement the High Level
 Committee recommendation in this regard.
AUDIT OF ACCOUNTS OF BRODER ROADS ORGANISATION
62.       The Committee observed that the brief on Border Roads Organisation supplied by BRDB did not consist of
 Audit Reports on the accounts of the Border Roads Organisation. The Committee enquired about the reasons therefor.
 In their reply, the representatives of Border Roads Organisation submitted before the Committee that the Border Roads
 Organisation is not a corporate Organisation where the accounts are audited. The Border Roads Organisation does not
 prepare balance sheets of profit and loss accounts. The accounts of Border Roads Organisation are audited by he
 Controller and Auditor General of Defence Accounts. The same rule, as applied to other departments, is applied while
 auditing of accounts of the Border Roads Organisation.
63.       The Committee is surprised to note that the Border Roads Organisation is spending the public money/funds but
 no auditing of accounts is being done by Comptroller and Auditor General of India. The Committee is of the view that
 if the account relating to similar activities of other Organisations are being audited by the Comptroller and Auditor
 General, then there is no justification for not getting the accounts of Border Roads Organisation audited in the similar
 way. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the accounts of the Border Roads Organisation should be got audited
 by the Comptroller and Auditor General, as is being done in the case of any other Government Organisations.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS AT A GLANCE
 
The Committee appreciates the functioning of Border roads Organisation in construction and maintenance of the border
 roads in the remote, inaccessible and far flung areas, which play vital role in operations of defence activities. The
 Committee also appreciates the works of Border Roads Organisation of summer snow clearance of the Srinagar-Zojila-
Leh and the Manali-Sarchu-Leh roads in time, which supplement the activities of the Armed forces. It also helped the
 Indian army to a great extent in success of “Operation Vijay” launched in Kargil during 1999. The work done by the
 BRO during that period was commendable.
(Para 19)
DEVELOPMENT OF NATIONAL HIGHWAYS BY BRODER ROADS ORGANISATION
The Committee is constrained to the note that the Border Roads Organisation has little or negligible participation in the
 National Highways Development Programme which is limited only to those National Highways which fall in difficult,
 inaccessible and remote areas of border States. The Border Roads Organisation has not been allowed competitive
 bidding for National Highways Projects and other State roads projects just because of it being a Central Government
 Organisation. The Committee is of the opinion that the National Highways Authority of India (NHAI) is yet to develop
 adequate institutional arrangements and therefore, it may not be possible for the NHAI to handle the National
 Highways Development Programme (NHDP) independently. On the other hand, the Border Roads Organisation is a
 well disciplined, motivated and the largest construction Organisation in the country equipped with proven capability
 and expertise developed over more than forty years in the area of the construction of roads, national highways,
 permanent bridges etc in border areas. The Committee has also been given impression that the potential of the Border
 Roads Organisation is not being fully exploited. The Committee, therefore, recommends that some mechanism be
 evolved which can ensure the participation of the Border roads Organisation in competitive bidding for National
 Highways projects and other state road projects. The Committee hopes that by increasing participation of Border Roads
 Organisation in NHDP and other state road projects, the country will be benefited by the expertise and experience of
 Border Roads Organisation in that area.
(Para 24)
The Border Roads Organisation plays vital role during the war and insurgent conditions. The Committee, however,
 constrained to note that the Organisation is facing crutch of funds for its General Staff works/projects. An amount of
 Rs. 338 crores per year was allocated exclusively for construction of General Staff Roads under the original General
 Staff Road perspective Plan 1997-2007. Thereafter, extra works have been assigned to the Border Roads Organisation.
 Consequent upon upgradation of General Staff Road Plan in 1999, addition of China Study Group roads and roads in
 Operation Vijay have put extra financial burden. The Committee is of the view that the amount of Rs. 338 crores per
 year being allocated annually to the Border Roads Organisation is highly inadequate to carry out all these works by
 Border Roads Organisation.
The Committee, therefore, recommends that the budgetary support to the General staff roads should be reviewed and
 enhanced to Rs. 540 crores per year as suggested by BRO and maintained till 2007 with a provision of 10 percent
 enhancement every year to cater to escalation so as to enable the Border roads Organisation complete the balance work
 by 2007.
(Paras 30 &31)
SHORTAGE OF EQUIPMENTS
The Committee is of the view that the level of funding for providing a reliable and sustainable level of plant, vehicle and
 construction equipments have not been adequate to fully meet the needs of the Organisation. Therefore, the Committee
 recommends that the allocation of adequate funds should be made available to the Border Roads Organisation for the
 coming financial years as to avoid deficiencies which might occur due to down gradation of plant, vehicles and
 equipments.

54th Report
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/54threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:53:12]
The Committee is pained to note that the Border Roads Organisation is holding equipments worth of Rs. 688.96 crores
 with a current depreciated value of Rs. 430.46 crores. The Committee is of the view that the unrepaired, accidental,
 premature and used equipments can be auctioned. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Organisation should
 proceed actively for the auction of machines and take special dispensation of the government to reduce the upset price
 where it is required, otherwise the machineries will deteriorate further and might become junk material. Further, the
 Organisation should, at regular internals, review the equipment and dispose of such items of machinery, which can no
 longer be used economically instead of building up of inventory of obsolete equipment.
(Paras 35 & 36)
SHORTAGE OF OFFICERS IN THE CIVIL ENGINEERING CADRE
The Committee is aware of the fact that the Border Roads Organisation personnel have to work under harsh and rough
 climatic conditions in hostile remote areas of borders. Sometime their lives are in danger or in miserable conditions.
 However, the concessions and facilities extended to these personnel are not adequate. It is pity that since inception
 Border Roads Organisation has not been paid any special attention to make the service conditions attractive in
 comparison to that of other Government departments as a result of which number of vacancies have remained unfilled
 coupled with frequent resignations in category of officers in Border Roads Organisation. The Committee notes with
 concern that even though the High level Committee had recommended for grant of North East concessions to its
 personnel at par with other Central government employees but the government has delinked the “North-East
 Concessions” from the Committee’s Report and process it separately without any justifiable reasons. The Committee,
 therefore, strongly recommends that the Government should on priority basis review their stand on the
 recommendations of High Level Committee keeping in view of the difficulties faced by the BRO personnel and
 consider the grant of all North-East concessions to the personnel of the Border Roads Organisation who are working in
 North East region.
The Committee is also of the view that the nature of work of Border Roads Organisation is of strategic importance to the
 nation and their work should not be allowed to suffer due to the shortage of officers/engineers in the Organisation. The
 working conditions in the Border Roads Organisation are relatively of difficult nature in comparison to other
 Government departments. The Committee finds no justification comparing status of BRO at par with other Government
 Organisations. The work of BRO is operational, technical and specialized and always play vital role in case of any
 emergency and war. The Committee, therefore, further recommends that the Border Roads Organisation should be
 given a special status and efforts be made to attract the talented professionals in the field by offering lucrative packages
 so that the Government can avoid and stop deficiency of officers in the BRO.
The Committee appreciates that despite shortage of officers, Border Roads Organisation has exceeded its targets in
 respect of formation, permanent works, permanent bridges etc.
(Paras 46,47 & 48)
SHORTAGE OF CLOTHING
The Committee feels sorry to note that there is shortage of clothing for GREF personnel. The GREF personnel are
 deployed in high altitude areas and working in highly uncongenial environment in the North East and Kashmir Valley,
 where the wear and tear is extremely high. In such conditions, the deficiency of clothing may not only affect the morale
 but also the performance of the personnel of Organisation. The cumulative effect of shortage of availability of funds
 has been that the annual requirement of funds is now about Rs. 27 crores. Against this requirement, the government has
 provided Rs. 18.50 crores and 20.50 crores during 2000-2001 and 2001-2002 respectively. The Committee strongly
 recommends that full requirement of funds for clothing is provided during the current year itself and in future adequate
 funding be provided for clothing.
(Para 51)
DEDICATED SECURITY COVER TO THE BORDER ROADS ORGANISATION
The Committee notes that the GREF personnel work in insurgent/Border areas, affected by the militancy, where
 equipments and GREF personnel are targeted. The Committee feels that the present security cover to the BRO
 personnel is inadequate which affects the projects. There is an urgent need for additional and adequate security cover to
 be provided to the GREF personnel. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the proposal of the Border Roads
 Organisation for sanction of creation of Territorial Army Battalions should be processed on priority and Territorial
 Army Battalions be formed at the earliest.
(Para 54)
MEDICAL FACILITIES AVAILABLE TO BRO PERSONNEL
The Committee observes that BRO personnel are deployed in remote, far-flung, inaccessible and difficult terrain but the
 existing medical facilities available to them are inadequate. No serious efforts have been made by the Government to

54th Report
file:///C/Users/user/Desktop/pri/Committee%20on%20Transport,%20Tourism%20and%20Culture/54threport.htm[28-08-2018 12:53:12]
 provide proper medical facilities. The Committee is constrained to note that at present only emergency medical
 facilities are available to BRO personnel at Zonal/Command Hospitals. The Committee therefore recommends that they
 should be provided general medical facilities in the hospitals of the Armed Forces considering BRO personnel just as
 members of the Armed Forces.
(Para 57)
COMPENSATION/EMPLOYMENT OT DEPENDENTS/WIDOWS OF BORDER ROADS ORGANISATION
 PERSONNEL
The Committee is constrained to note the indifferent attitude of the Government towards the widows and dependents of
 Border Roads Organisation personnel who laid down their lives while serving the Organisation. More than 156 cases
 for employment on compassionate ground are still pending. The Committee, therefore, recommends that these cases
 should be expeditiously settled and employment should be provided to the next kin of the deceased personnel of Border
 Roads Organisation. Possibility should be explored that the widows of the deceased personnel should be posted at
 nearby places so that their family life is not disturbed.
The Committee is unhappy to note that the personnel of the Border Roads Organisation are being discriminated in case
 of compensation on death due to accident or hostilities. Therefore, the Committee recommends that compensation
 should be given to the families of the deceased BRO personnel at par with that given in the case of other Central
 Government Organisation/Departments and Government should also give priority to implement the High Level
 Committee recommendation in this regard.
(Para 60 & 61)
AUDIT OF ACCOUNTS OF BORDER ROADS ORGANISATION
The Committee is surprised to note that the Border Roads Organisation is spending the public money/funds but no
 auditing of accounts is being done by Comptroller and Auditor General of India. The Committee is of the view that if
 the account relating to similar activities of other Organisations are being audited by the Comptroller and Auditor
 General, then there is no justification for not getting the accounts of Border Roads Organisation audited in the similar
 way. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the accounts of the Border Roads Organisation should be got audited
 by the Comptroller and Auditor General, as is being done in the case of any other Government Organisations.
(Para 63)

 INTRODUCTION
 
The Department of Tourism, in the Ministry of Tourism and Culture, is the nodal agency for the formulation of
 national policies and programmes and for the coordination of activities of various Central Government Agencies, State
 Governments/Union Territories and the Private Sector for the development and promotion of tourism in the country.  The
 role of the Department of Tourism has been to coordinate and supplement the efforts of the State/U.T. Governments in
 development of tourism through Central financial assistance, to catalyze private investment, strengthen promotional and
 marketing efforts and to provide trained manpower resources. The main activities of the Department are:-
 
(i)
                   Policy formulation and planning
(ii)                  Co-ordination
(iii)                Regulation
(iv)                Infrastructure and Product development
(v)                  Human Resource Development
(vi)                Publicity, Marketing and Facilitation
(vii)               Research, Analysis, Monitoring and Evaluation
(viii)              International Co-operation and External Assistance
(ix)                Legislation and Parliament work
(x)                  Management of Public Sector Undertakings and Autonomous bodies
 
2.       The administrative head of the Department is the Secretary (Tourism).  The Department is assisted by an attached
 office headed by the Director General.  The office of the Director General of Tourism provides executive directions for the
 implementation of various policies and programmes.  Directorate General of Tourism has a field formation of 21 offices
 within the country and 18 offices abroad.  The overseas offices are primarily responsible for tourism promotion and
 marketing in their respective areas and the field offices in India are responsible for providing information service to tourists
 and to monitor the progress of field projects.
 
3.       The Department of Tourism has the following public sector undertaking/autonomous institutions under its
 administrative control:-
 
a)            India Tourism Development Corporation Limited (ITDC);
b)           National Council for Hotel Management and Catering Technology and the Institutes under its control (NCHMCT)
c)            Indian Institute of Tourism & Travel Management (IITTM);
d)           Indian Institute of Skiing & Mountaineering (IISM);
e)            National Institute of Water Sports (NIWS).

(ii)      Attempts to harness the direct and multiplier effects of tourism for employment generation, economic development and
 providing impetus to rural tourism:
(iii)     Provide a major thrust to domestic tourism which will act as a spring board for growth and expansion of international
 tourism;
(iv)     Position India as a global brand to take advantage of the burgeoning global travel and trade and the vast untapped
 potential of India as a destination;
(v)      Acknowledge the critical role of private sector with government working as an active facilitator and catalyst;
(vi)     Create and develop integrated tourism circuits based on India's unique civilisation, heritage and culture in partnership
 with states, private sector with and other agencies;
 (vii)   Ensure that the tourist to India gets physically invigorated, mentally rejuvenated, culturally enriched, spiritually
 elevated and "feels India within him".

 for the disinvestment of one particular hotel, how could the atmosphere be considered as conducive for disinvestment of
 other hotels?  In such a scenario, the disinvestment of the hotels of ITDC may not fetch the actual commercial value of these
 properties.  The Committee recommends that instead of disinvestment, the Government should explore the possibility of
 giving these hotels on a long-term lease.  In this way the Government will not be losing the asset value of the hotel properties

 would be given to promote village tourism as the primary tourism product to spread tourism and its socio-economic benefits
 to rural and its new geographic regions.  Key geographic regions would be identified for development and promotion of rural
 tourism.  The implementation would be done through a conversance Committee headed by the District Collector.  A sum of
 Rs.20 lakhs would be made available for each project and activities like improving the environment, hygiene, infrastructure
 etc. would be eligible for assistance.
 
52.     The Committee enquired from the representatives of the Department of Tourism how they proposed to develop Rural
 Tourism and what projects had been conceived in this regard?  The Committee also desired to know the steps taken to
 provide road connectivity in the areas identified for development of tourism.
 
53.     Giving the details about 'Rural Tourism', the Secretary (Tourism) explained to the Committee that it was a new
 concept.  She informed that the Department was going to take up five pilot projects of Rural Tourism.  She clarified that the
 Department was yet to define their own model of Rural Tourism.  They would aim not only to attract Indian and foreign
 tourists but also take into account the marketing aspect as well as the environment aspect.  As regards road connectivity, it
 was informed that they had been in constant touch with the roadways department.
 
54.     The Committee appreciates the idea of the Department of Tourism in developing Rural Tourism. The Committee feels
 that the concept of Rural Tourism would also help in generation of employment at the rural level, dispensing with the need of
 migration to distant places for earning of livelihood by the people living in the rural areas.  However, the Committee feels
 that the infrastructural facilities like road connectivity, wayside amenities etc. are essential in the development of such kind
 of tourism.  While taking steps for development of Rural Tourism, the Department of Tourism should simultaneously take
 steps for developing the infrastructural facilities in these areas.
 
THE NEW TOURISM POLICY
 
55.     As regards the new Tourism Policy, the Department of Tourism have informed that the Draft New Tourism Policy was
 discussed in a conference of all the Chief Ministers and Tourism Ministers and that the New Tourism Policy was under
 finalisation.  The New Tourism Policy will provide thrust on development of new tourist products like rural tourism, eco-
